8	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
9	9.1 Laws of Sports Mastery: Principles of Training
10	Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky 
11	Translated from the Russian by Dr. Michael Yessis 
12	With assistance from Natalia Verkhoshansky
13	Introduction
14	As established many years ago (Verkhoshansky, 13,18), the multi year Process of Achieving 
15	Sports Mastery (PASM) was developed on a base of definite laws. Athletes can achieve the 
16	heights of sports mastery by different pathways and expend different amounts of time doing this. 
17	However, the path taken by each athlete will have general traits, inherent to all athletes. These 
18	general characteristics are determined by the biological nature of man: genetically imposed abili­
19	ties of the body to accommodate to the changing conditions of his existence (Verkhoshansky, 
20	13,18, 26, 27). It is mainly because of this that specialists in the area of sports science have been 
21	giving more attention to biological knowledge (Verkhoshansky, 17, 26, 27, Viru, 32, 291, 
22	Yakovlev, 143, 144, Viru. Kirge, 35, Tschine, 277, Neuman, 253). They are striving to find the 
23	key to further deepening the principles of preparation of high level athletes.
24	Russian (Yakovlev, 143, 144, Viru, 32, 60, 62, Gippenreiter, 43, Medvedev, 73, Kasnacheev, 59, 
25	Garkavi. 42) and foreign (Booth, 160, Darnel et al., 186, Williams et al., 298, Underwood, Wil­
26	liams, 278, Seedorf et al., 269, Galbo. 203) representatives of the biological sciences (including 
27	molecular and cellular biology), see possibilities for using their achievements and methods to 
28	study the adaptation process during sports activity: the mechanisms that control the interactions 
29	of different systems in the body during single physical loads as well as the mechanisms of adap­
30	tation to multiple repetitive (systematic) training sessions. According to them, this makes it pos­
31	sible to broaden the limits of man’s abilities and by this, to work out training programs at new 
32	qualitative levels (Booth, 160, Viru, 290, 291, Yakovlev, 143).
33	The general Theory of Adaptation plays a central role in this (123, 134, Meerson, 74, 75, Garka­
34	vi. 42, Slonim, 106, Kasnacheev. 59, Kusnetzov, 68, Medvedev, 73, Yakivlev, 144). Part of this 
35	theory is in regard to the process of human adaptation to conditions of loaded muscular activity, 
36	including sports activities (Meerson, 74, 75, Viru. 32, 33, 291, Kassil, 60, Yakovlev, 138, Verk­
37	hoshansky, Viru, 28, 286, Viru, Kirge, 35).
38	Adaptation appears when the surrounding conditions change to such an extent that they cease to 
39	be adequate to maintain stability of the human organism. This includes both the body's genetic 
40	construction (genotype) as well as its actual observed properties (phenotype). The basis for the 
41	mechanism of adaptation consists of the complex (set) of the whole (total) body reactions, di­
42	rected to maintaining or restoring homeostasis, in response to the changed conditions of the sur­
43	roundings (134, Meerson, 76, 77, Haydarliu, 124, Kasnacheev, 59, Kusnetzov, 68, Yakovlev, 
44	144 ’).
45	The base mechanism and structure of the adaptation process, at the level of biochemical, func­
46	tional and morphological restructuring in the body, are convincingly described in the multiple
47	1 See also the book “Components of the adaptation process”. Edition of V.I. Medvedev, Nauka, 1984, 109 pp.
48	504
49	
50	=====PDF 516 / p.505=====
51	SUPERTRs\INING ADDENDUM
52	publications of experimental and theoretical research results (Selye, 271, Meerson, 74, Kas- 
53	nacheev, 59, Viru, 291, Kassil, 60, Kassil et al., 61, Haydarliu, 124, Panin. 94).
54	In these studies:
55	1) it was found that the concept o f the stress-syndrome, formulated as a non-specific compo­
56	nent of the adaptive reaction, ensures the attraction of energy and plastic reserves for realiza­
57	tion of specific adaptational restructuring of the body;
58	2) were clarified the ideas about:
59	- 
60	the particularities of the interactions between the specific homeostatic reactions and the 
61	general non-specific adaptive reactions;
62	- 
63	the mechanism of the transfer from short term (acute) adaptation to long term adaptation 
64	through activation of the genetic apparatus of the cells and the induction of adaptive pro­
65	tein synthesis;
66	the relationship between the processes of mobilization of the energy and plastic sources 
67	in the human body.
68	The results of these research studies show that there are two stages in development of the adap­
69	tational process: the beginning stage - “acute" (short term), incomplete adaptation, and the fol­
70	lowing stage - “long term'’, completed adaptation (Kusnetzov, 68, Meerson, 74, 77, Haydarliu, 
71	124, Viru, 32 ). The beginning stage of the adaptive reaction starts immediately after the external 
72	impact (the influence of some irritant) beginning and, for this reason, could be realized only on 
73	the basis of the earlier formed physiological mechanisms that are ready to respond immediately. 
74	The most important trait of this stage of adaptation is that the activity of the body takes place on 
75	the limits of its physiological abilities, during almost full mobilization of the functional reserves, 
76	which are still far from the full measure needed to ensure the necessary adaptational effect.
77	The “long tern r stage of adaptation appears gradually as a result of long or multiple repetitions 
78	of influences on the body by some factors in the surrounding environment. It is developed on the 
79	basis of multiple realizations of “acute" adaptation and is characterized by the total gradual quan­
80	titative accumulation of some changes in the body so that it acquires a new quality - a level of 
81	functional abilities that is greater than earlier and more adequate for the athlete's current re­
82	quirements (Meerson, 76, 77, Haydarliu, 124, Kaznacheev, 59 ).
83	The transition from the “short term" to the “long term"' state, shows a the main moment in the 
84	adaptational process, that is, it is essentially this transition that makes it possible to have constant 
85	life of the organism in new conditions and widens the sphere of his habitat and freedom of carry­
86	ing on in a changing biological and social sphere (Meerson, 77, Kaznacheev, 59).
87	Studies in the last decades, dealing with very different objectives but using one and the same 
88	complex of methods, showed that an increase in the function of organs and systems naturally en­
89	tail the activation of the synthesis of nucleic acid and cell proteins that form these organs and 
90	systems. Such activation leads to the formation of structural (morphological) changes which 
91	mainly increase the power of the systems responsible for adaptation and appear as a quality ma­
92	terial base on which the formation and transition from “short" to “long term" adaptation is real­
93	ized.
94	505
95	
96	=====PDF 517 / p.506=====
97	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
98	The “long term" adaptation mechanism is comprised of the energy and plastic providing func­
99	tions of the body together with their mutual conditioning effect. The energy ensuring function is 
100	seen in the joining of the metabolic processes, as a result of which, a sufficient amount of energy 
101	for realizing the functional activity on the needed level, is formed and released. The plastic pro­
102	vision is a process of repair of the functional, energy forming, transport and support structures of 
103	the cells. It is realized through protein biosynthesis that ensures stability of the physiological 
104	functions of the whole body (Viru, 32, Meerson, 76, 77, Haydarliu, 124. Panin. 94).
105	The human body represents a biological system. According to E.Bauer2 (Bauer, 4, Kasnacheev, 
106	59), the state of the biological system is determined by interaction between two main energy 
107	flows: the first is used to attain the maximal effect of “external work” (energy ensuring function), 
108	and the second flow is used to attain restitution of the energy ensuring macro- and micro struc­
109	tures (plastic provision function) (Kaznacheev, 59).
110	The course taken and the result 
111	of the “adaptational behavior” 
112	of the body, is determined by 
113	the interaction and optimal cor­
114	relation of these processes (see 
115	Figure 1).
116	If in the stable body state, when 
117	the adaptogenic factor is absent 
118	and the mechanism of adapta­
119	tion is not activated, these proc­
120	esses are realized (function) 
121	within normal limits of physio­
122	logical fluctuations (see Figure 
123	1 graph a). When the adapto­
124	genic factor is present (inade­
125	quate conditions in the envi­
126	ronment) the amplitude of oscil­
127	lation in the alternation of the
128	Figure 1 - Interaction between the energy flows in the biological systems 
129	(V.P. Kasnacheev, 1980)
130	The relative energy share:
131	I - to achieve the maximal effect of external work,
132	II - to obtain the micro- and macro-structures restitution; 
133	a - the normal correlation,
134	b and c - the compensational limits.
135	“ Erwin Bauer (1890-I938). Austro-Hungarian biologist, defined the essence of life as a steady non-equilibrium 
136	state. According to the Bauer’s "principle of the permanent non-equilibrium of living matter", the particularity of 
137	the life events is maintained by the substances exchange processes in the living organisms which need the constant 
138	energy consumption: “Living systems could never be in equilibrium, they constantly use their “free” energy, 
139	working against equilibrium, determined by the physical and chemical lows, actual for their current environment 
140	(E. Bauer “ Theoretical Biology”. Moscow-Leningrad, 1935, page 43).
141	Erwin Bauer formulated two general biological lows:
142	1. Development of biological systems is the result of increasing of their external working effect (the organism's 
143	impact on environment) in response to the stimulus (unit of energy), received from environment. For this 
144	reason, biological systems able to maintain the constancy of their structure independently form external envi­
145	ronment.
146	2. Since the biological systems are constantly working and destructing, they must be able to recover themselves, 
147	bringing from environment all necessary materials, energy and information. Thanks to this auto-restoration 
148	process, biological systems maintain the “anti-entropic” condition in relation to the environment which they 
149	live.
150	506
151	
152	=====PDF 518 / p.507=====
153	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
154	energetic and plastic providing functions increases. However, it is only up to a certain physio­
155	logical limit after which there inevitably is a disturbance in the adaptational mechanism (Bauer, 
156	4, Kasnacheev, 59). However, in separate stages one or another process can dominate, and even 
157	in micro intervals of time, a balance between them is maintained.
158	Management of the adaptation process is done by the CNS (Figure 2).
159	The first results of this activity appear in the activation of specific homeostatic reactions (Figure
160	2). When the strength (level) of the irritants is not high and the changes in the external and inter­
161	nal environment is not great, and in the presence of the previously worked out adaptation to a 
162	given action, the adaptational effect is limited to the specifics of the homeostatic reactions. Ful­
163	fillment of these reactions, the same as in any life activity, requires energy and plastic provi­
164	sional functions.
165	The first to begin this task is fulfillment of the energy capabilities and plastic reserve of cell 
166	function. However, according to the amount of increase in strength and duration of the influence 
167	and the intensity of the life activity acts that are fulfilled, the energy and plastic capabilities of
168	Figure 2 - The scheme of the mechanism of general adaptation (Viru, 1981)
169	507
170	
171	=====PDF 519 / p.508=====
172	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
173	individual cells require support from the side of general mobilization of the energy and plastic 
174	reserves of the body. This means mobilization of the non-specific component of adaptation or 
175	(according to Viru) inclusion of the general adaptation mechanism.
176	Activation of the non-specific component of adaptation appears as the basic sign of the stress 
177	state, i.e., the state of the body characterized by the display of the general adaptation mechanism 
178	which ensures the positive background for realization of specific homeostatic reactions and mo­
179	bilization of the defensive effort by the body (Meerson. 75, 76, 77, Viru, 32, 291. Yakovlev, 
180	144).
181	In this way the basic component of the general adaptation mechanism appears as mobilization of 
182	the energy resources of the body and the energy provision function, mobilization of the plastic 
183	resources of the body and adaptive synthesis of enzymes and structural proteins. It also includes 
184	mobilization of the defense abilities of the body. These components are directed by the interac­
185	tion of different hormonal systems and the immediate nervous influences, including the nerve- 
186	trophic action and activation of the trophic systems (Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Haydarliu, 124, 
187	Kassil, 62, Kassil et al., 61. Meerson, 77).
188	In mobilization of the energy resources of the body and in the energy provision function, pre­
189	dominant importance is given to the sympatho-adrenal system, the influence of which is reached 
190	in the tissues with the help of its hormonal (adrenaline) and mediatory (noradrenaline) links. 
191	Mobilization of the plastic reserve of the body under stress is a function of the hypophyseal- 
192	adrenocortical system. It is locked in with the creation of a free amino acid reserve for the plas­
193	tic ensuring function, that is, adaptive synthesis of proteins (Viru, 32, 289, Viru. Kirge, 35, Ya­
194	kovlev, 144).
195	One of the essentials of adaptational restructuring is that in the adaptive body, there is increased 
196	power of the mechanism of the hormonal - humoral regulation (Viru, 32, 291, Bunt, 166, Ver- 
197	voom, 287, Kasssil, 61). This gives advance notice of the exhaustion of resources during long 
198	term hyper-functioning and with this, makes it possible to create the ability to adequately supply 
199	long maintenance hormonally. In addition, it increases the maximum reaction of the body to limit 
200	loads, that ensures maximum mobilization of its functional capabilities (Viru,32, 291, Booth, 
201	160, Galbo, 203, Viru, Kirge, 35, Kassil, 60, Kassil ed al. 61, Haydarliu, 124).
202	It has been proven that the unique correct path to the formulation of effective practical principles 
203	of sports training is through the clarification of the laws of human body adaptation to loaded 
204	muscular activity as well as the laws of the process of achieving sports mastery (PASM) in line 
205	with the analytical conclusions of multi-year practical experiences (Verkhoshansky, 21, 25, 
206	Verkhoshansky, Viru, 28, 286, Yakovlev, 139, 143).
207	The vastness and basic orientation of the scientific search in this area and their methodological 
208	hierarchy have already been determined (Verkhoshansky, 21. 24 - 27).
209	The general laws of PASM are first of all determined by the laws of development of the adapta­
210	tional process related to sports activity (Figure 3).
211	To a good extent, an increase in sports mastery is determined by a whole line of factors—socio­
212	economic conditions, effectiveness of the theoretical concept of training, professional mastery of 
213	the coach, the individual psycho-physiological personality traits of the athlete and so on. How-
214	508
215	
216	=====PDF 520 / p.509=====
217	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
218	Figure 3 - The principal structure of the fundamentals of the Theory and Methodology of Sport Training
219	ever, even with the indubitable significance of these factors, they are secondary. They can be 
220	looked at (and realized) under the process of PASM, but do not determine the principle mecha­
221	nisms of its development.
222	The general laws of the PASM reflect the necessary structure of multiyear training in an objec­
223	tive manner, including the order of development of all of its components and the principles of 
224	their interactions. Here we have in view the laws of the morpho-functional specialization and the 
225	formation of technical-tactical mastery. The methodological ideas and their organization are ab­
226	stracted from all the joint parts of the PASM laws, the principles of training etc. In turn, these 
227	principles are joined with the objective display of the practical realization of the laws of adapta­
228	tion of the body to loaded muscular activity, to determine the organizational-temporal form of 
229	constructing sports training (Verkhoshansky, 26, 27).
230	1. Specific essentials of the adaptation process during sports activity
231	Development of long term adaptation during sports activity reveals many specific traits. Clarifi­
232	cation of these traits has great significance in the formation of the theoretical understanding of 
233	PASM and the methodological principles of training
234	509
235	
236	=====PDF 521 / p.510=====
237	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
238	1.1. 
239	Understanding compensator}' adaptation
240	Short term adaptation transitions gradually into long term on the basis o f multiple short term and 
241	systematic training effects on the body (training days, training sessions). In this, there is multiple 
242	short term repetition of the excess distribution of the body's plastic reserves that are used for re­
243	pair of the physiologically worn out structures, as well as for adaptive synthesis of structural and 
244	enzymatic proteins, ensuring temporary increases in the ability of the cells to do more active 
245	functioning. As a result of long term repetition, the effects of these changes are strengthened and 
246	become more expressed. In this way, in place of the temporary redistribution of the plastic re­
247	serves of the body during short term adaptation, there is development of stable, stronger reforma- 
248	tion-long term adaptive restructuring (Verkhoshansky, Viru. 28 Viru. 32).
249	In the foundation of temporary over-distribution of the plastic reserves of the body are the com­
250	pensatory mechanisms, that is, familiar reactions directed to maintaining the necessary level of 
251	body functioning during inadequate conditions that are sufficient for development of a stable 
252	form of adaptation. The compensatory mechanisms are dynamic and quickly rising physiologi­
253	cal means of breakdown in order to provide for the body in extreme conditions and to gradually 
254	extinguish these means according to the amount of development of stable long term adaptation. 
255	In as much as these mechanisms precede the latter, they can be looked at as pre-adaptation ap­
256	pearances (Kusnetzov, 68).
257	In this way there is a greater base on which to speak of the compensatory adaptation that appears 
258	as a quality prerequisite and condition for development of stable long term adaptation (Verkho­
259	shansky, 25). The latter can have a progressive character if the training influence is stressful and 
260	brings about systematic disturbance of body homeostasis, and if the morphological restructuring 
261	of the body in the process of compensatory adaptation appears to be sufficiently substantial, in 
262	order to significantly influence the established external and internal relationships of the body, it 
263	brings the body to a new, higher level of special workability (Verkhoshansky, Viru. 28, 286).
264	1.2. 
265	Current adaptation reserv es of the body
266	The phase of compensatory adaptation is characterized by intense mobilization of the energy and 
267	plastic reserves of the body. This phase cannot be long. The accumulation in the body of worn 
268	out and “defeated" structures requires higher mobilization of the plastic reserves which leads to a 
269	decrease in the effect of the external work. After some time, the body recovers its functions up 
270	to a level which significantly surpasses the initial (Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Viru, 289). This 
271	signifies restoration of its adaptation potential and its readiness to once again accommodate reor­
272	ganization to extreme influences (Verkhoshansky,Viru, 28, 286).
273	This is the beginning hypothesis of the current adaptation reserve (CAR), which the body always 
274	has available for extreme situations that may arise requiring maximum functional loading (Verk­
275	hoshansky, 1985- 24, 1988 - 282, 1993 - 27). This means that the body is always ready to re­
276	spond to stronger external influences with adequate accommodation restructuring and to move 
277	on to a new functional level of motor abilities (Verkhoshansky, Viru. 28, 286). The volume of 
278	CAR has a definite limit, which is conditional (as determined from specialized studies) based on 
279	two factors: the adaptation (functional) reserve of the sympathetic-adrenal and hypophysial - 
280	adrenocorticoid systems (Viru, 32), and the absolute level of adaptation (morpho-functional) re­
281	structuring. which has already been realized in the body at the present time (Verkho-
282	510
283	
284	=====PDF 522 / p.511=====
285	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
286	shansky.Viru, 28, 286). With an increase in sport mastery, that is, according to the degree of ap­
287	proaching the genetically conditioned limit of adaptation capabilities, the volume of CAR de­
288	creases (Verkhoshansky, 24, 27, 282).
289	The task of compensatory adaptation is locked into the use of CAR for maintaining the hyper 
290	functions (Verkhoshansky, 25, 26, 27). The realization of CAR to the limits that it can be with­
291	stood, activates the genetic apparatus of inner cellular regulation, which carries with it activation 
292	of nucleic acid synthesis and proteins in the cells of the organs and systems that answer to adap­
293	tation. Such activation leads to the formation of structural (morphological) changes, that mainly 
294	increase the functional power of these systems, ensuring the transition from short term adaptation 
295	to long term (Meerson. 76-77, Viru, 32,33). In this, there is restoration of the adaptation reserves 
296	of the body, which in turn, prepares it for a new hyper-function that is, to engage extreme condi­
297	tions (Verkhoshansky,Viru, 28, 286).
298	As brought out earlier, the presence of the adaptation reserve in the body is seen in cases of acci­
299	dents (wrecks) (Yakovlev, 137, Prokop, 258, Beckman, 154, Letunov, 154, Garkavi, 42). Fre­
300	quently, even at the end of the 1950's, the concept of adaptation energy (adaptation ability) dis­
301	bursement during stress, together with its possible restoration, w'as used to explain the dynamics 
302	of sports achievements during training. Three phases were determined:
303	1. Phase of adaptation (increase in the athlete's abilities);
304	2. Phase of the highest sports workability;
305	3. Phase of readaptation (Prokop. 258)3.

384	Specificity of protein synthesis during adaptation
385	Systematic loaded muscle activity is tied in with greater mobilization of energy resources that 
386	require activation of the plastic provision function of the body (Meerson, 76, 77, 78, Yakovlev, 
387	144, 124, Panin, 94, Viru, 289). The plastic provisions include renewal of proteins, strengthening 
388	cell structure functioning, long term synthesis of enzymatic proteins and the protein synthesis 
389	necessary for the amino acids and precursors of nucleic acid (Viru, 32, Kassil, 60,61, Yakovlev, 
390	140, 144, Haidarliu. 124, Viru, 288. Breitbart et all, 163).
391	Synthesis of proteins is provided for by the genetic program coordinated in the nucleus of the 
392	cell. Its realization activates the action of the inductors (Yakovlev, 144. Viru, 291, Booth, 160, 
393	Miwa et all, 247, Horton, 227, Bylund-Fellenius, 169, Breitbart et all, 163). The basic inductors 
394	appear to be the cell metabolites (products of substance exchange in the cells) and hormones, 
395	reaching the cells via the blood (Poortemans, 257, Viru. 289, 32).
396	Metabolites determine the specific character of the protein synthesis; synthesized are those pro­
397	teins which are primarily destroyed, and likewise enzymes catalyzing biochemical reactions, ly­
398	ing in the base of the corresponding functions. With this, specific correspondence between func­
399	tional activity and adaptation of protein synthesis is ensured. Hormones as a rule strengthen 
400	adaptive protein synthesis, inducted by metabolites (Yakovlev, 138, 139, 140, Viru, 32, 291, 
401	Viru, Kirge, 35, Haidarliu, 124).
402	Thus, the catabolic processes that take place in the muscles during the time of work determine 
403	the specific character of the following biosynthesis of the substances destroyed during muscular 
404	activity, that is, the specificity of the anabolic processes that take place in the post work period 
405	(Yakovlev. 144, Breitbart et all, 163, Booth et all, 159).

646	Essentials of the constructive effects of the adaptational process
647	The foundation for the development of the adaptational process in sports activity is the strength­
648	ened synthesis of structural and enzymatic proteins in the actively functioning cells. This is car­
649	ried out through the structural reformation toward greater functional power of the cell structure 
650	and with this, the tissues, organs and the entire body (Yakovlev, 140, 144. Viru. 32, 289, 291, 
651	Viru, Kirge, 35, Bylund-Fellenius et al., 169, Booth, 160). The pathway to stronger and purpose­
652	fully directed synthesis of proteins in the body takes place from the short adaptive reactions in 
653	long term adaptation (Meerson, 74, Viru, 33, 289). Strengthened protein synthesis as a natural 
654	life providing reaction of the body in response to extreme influences and the piling up of plastic 
655	process content (Meerson, 76,77, Haydarliu,124, Panin, 94) appears as a constructive effect of 
656	the adaptational process (Verkhoshansky, 24,25, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 28, Viru, 33).
657	The basis for the constructive effect of adaptation lies in three phenomena (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 
658	32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286):
659	specificity of protein synthesis in the after work period, conditioned by the character of the 
660	work executed, its intensity and means of energy provision,
661	- 
662	supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates 
663	serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins),
664	- 
665	a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the 
666	muscular work.
667	In this way, the known laws of development of the adaptational process during sports activity 
668	makes it possible to speak of two levels of the constructive effect. (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, 
669	Verkhoshansky, Viru, 28, 286). One of them is related to the well known phase of restitution that 
670	is inherent in the phenomenon of supercompensation of products and energy used up in external 
671	work (Yakovlev, 139, 144, Viru, 289). The other level is related to the long stages of training. It 
672	is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a 
673	result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect 
674	(Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283).
675	As stated above, the phase of restitution is characterized not only by increased metabolism but 
676	also a higher turnover speed of the muscle proteins which ensures the renewal of the molecular 
677	composition of the actin - myosin complex and other muscular proteins, in order to eliminate the 
678	“physiologically exhausted” structural “footprints” structural elements and guarantee a high reli­
679	ability of the contractile function (Viru, 289, 291).
680	The program of biochemical changes which are carried out as a result of the muscle exercise, de­
681	termine the catabolic processes taking place in the muscles during the time of work. This pro­
682	gram is realized during the time of rest, when the processes of anabolic-biosynthesis of products 
683	expended during muscle activity, takes place (Yakovlev, 138, 144, Viru, 31, 32, 33, 289).

9.1 Laws of Sports Mastery: Principles of Training
Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky 
Translated from the Russian by Dr. Michael Yessis 
With assistance from Natalia Verkhoshansky
Introduction
As established many years ago (Verkhoshansky, 13,18), the multi year Process of Achieving 
Sports Mastery (PASM) was developed on a base of definite laws. Athletes can achieve the 
heights of sports mastery by different pathways and expend different amounts of time doing this. 
However, the path taken by each athlete will have general traits, inherent to all athletes. These 
general characteristics are determined by the biological nature of man: genetically imposed abili­
ties of the body to accommodate to the changing conditions of his existence (Verkhoshansky, 
13,18, 26, 27). It is mainly because of this that specialists in the area of sports science have been 
giving more attention to biological knowledge (Verkhoshansky, 17, 26, 27, Viru, 32, 291, 
Yakovlev, 143, 144, Viru. Kirge, 35, Tschine, 277, Neuman, 253). They are striving to find the 
key to further deepening the principles of preparation of high level athletes.
Russian (Yakovlev, 143, 144, Viru, 32, 60, 62, Gippenreiter, 43, Medvedev, 73, Kasnacheev, 59, 
Garkavi. 42) and foreign (Booth, 160, Darnel et al., 186, Williams et al., 298, Underwood, Wil­
liams, 278, Seedorf et al., 269, Galbo. 203) representatives of the biological sciences (including 
molecular and cellular biology), see possibilities for using their achievements and methods to 
study the adaptation process during sports activity: the mechanisms that control the interactions 
of different systems in the body during single physical loads as well as the mechanisms of adap­
tation to multiple repetitive (systematic) training sessions. According to them, this makes it pos­
sible to broaden the limits of man’s abilities and by this, to work out training programs at new 
qualitative levels (Booth, 160, Viru, 290, 291, Yakovlev, 143).
The general Theory of Adaptation plays a central role in this (123, 134, Meerson, 74, 75, Garka­
vi. 42, Slonim, 106, Kasnacheev. 59, Kusnetzov, 68, Medvedev, 73, Yakivlev, 144). Part of this 
theory is in regard to the process of human adaptation to conditions of loaded muscular activity, 
including sports activities (Meerson, 74, 75, Viru. 32, 33, 291, Kassil, 60, Yakovlev, 138, Verk­
hoshansky, Viru, 28, 286, Viru, Kirge, 35).
Adaptation appears when the surrounding conditions change to such an extent that they cease to 
be adequate to maintain stability of the human organism. This includes both the body's genetic 
construction (genotype) as well as its actual observed properties (phenotype). The basis for the 
mechanism of adaptation consists of the complex (set) of the whole (total) body reactions, di­
rected to maintaining or restoring homeostasis, in response to the changed conditions of the sur­
roundings (134, Meerson, 76, 77, Haydarliu, 124, Kasnacheev, 59, Kusnetzov, 68, Yakovlev, 
144 ’).
The base mechanism and structure of the adaptation process, at the level of biochemical, func­
tional and morphological restructuring in the body, are convincingly described in the multiple
1 See also the book “Components of the adaptation process”. Edition of V.I. Medvedev, Nauka, 1984, 109 pp.
504

publications of experimental and theoretical research results (Selye, 271, Meerson, 74, Kas- 
nacheev, 59, Viru, 291, Kassil, 60, Kassil et al., 61, Haydarliu, 124, Panin. 94).
In these studies:
1) it was found that the concept o f the stress-syndrome, formulated as a non-specific compo­
nent of the adaptive reaction, ensures the attraction of energy and plastic reserves for realiza­
tion of specific adaptational restructuring of the body;
2) were clarified the ideas about:
- 
the particularities of the interactions between the specific homeostatic reactions and the 
general non-specific adaptive reactions;
- 
the mechanism of the transfer from short term (acute) adaptation to long term adaptation 
through activation of the genetic apparatus of the cells and the induction of adaptive pro­
tein synthesis;
the relationship between the processes of mobilization of the energy and plastic sources 
in the human body.
The results of these research studies show that there are two stages in development of the adap­
tational process: the beginning stage - “acute" (short term), incomplete adaptation, and the fol­
lowing stage - “long term'’, completed adaptation (Kusnetzov, 68, Meerson, 74, 77, Haydarliu, 
124, Viru, 32 ). The beginning stage of the adaptive reaction starts immediately after the external 
impact (the influence of some irritant) beginning and, for this reason, could be realized only on 
the basis of the earlier formed physiological mechanisms that are ready to respond immediately. 
The most important trait of this stage of adaptation is that the activity of the body takes place on 
the limits of its physiological abilities, during almost full mobilization of the functional reserves, 
which are still far from the full measure needed to ensure the necessary adaptational effect.
The “long tern r stage of adaptation appears gradually as a result of long or multiple repetitions 
of influences on the body by some factors in the surrounding environment. It is developed on the 
basis of multiple realizations of “acute" adaptation and is characterized by the total gradual quan­
titative accumulation of some changes in the body so that it acquires a new quality - a level of 
functional abilities that is greater than earlier and more adequate for the athlete's current re­
quirements (Meerson, 76, 77, Haydarliu, 124, Kaznacheev, 59 ).
The transition from the “short term" to the “long term"' state, shows a the main moment in the 
adaptational process, that is, it is essentially this transition that makes it possible to have constant 
life of the organism in new conditions and widens the sphere of his habitat and freedom of carry­
ing on in a changing biological and social sphere (Meerson, 77, Kaznacheev, 59).
Studies in the last decades, dealing with very different objectives but using one and the same 
complex of methods, showed that an increase in the function of organs and systems naturally en­
tail the activation of the synthesis of nucleic acid and cell proteins that form these organs and 
systems. Such activation leads to the formation of structural (morphological) changes which 
mainly increase the power of the systems responsible for adaptation and appear as a quality ma­
terial base on which the formation and transition from “short" to “long term" adaptation is real­
ized.
505

=====PDF 517 / p.506=====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
The “long term" adaptation mechanism is comprised of the energy and plastic providing func­
tions of the body together with their mutual conditioning effect. The energy ensuring function is 
seen in the joining of the metabolic processes, as a result of which, a sufficient amount of energy 
for realizing the functional activity on the needed level, is formed and released. The plastic pro­
vision is a process of repair of the functional, energy forming, transport and support structures of 
the cells. It is realized through protein biosynthesis that ensures stability of the physiological 
functions of the whole body (Viru, 32, Meerson, 76, 77, Haydarliu, 124. Panin. 94).
The human body represents a biological system. According to E.Bauer2 (Bauer, 4, Kasnacheev, 
59), the state of the biological system is determined by interaction between two main energy 
flows: the first is used to attain the maximal effect of “external work” (energy ensuring function), 
and the second flow is used to attain restitution of the energy ensuring macro- and micro struc­
tures (plastic provision function) (Kaznacheev, 59).
The course taken and the result 
of the “adaptational behavior” 
of the body, is determined by 
the interaction and optimal cor­
relation of these processes (see 
Figure 1).
If in the stable body state, when 
the adaptogenic factor is absent 
and the mechanism of adapta­
tion is not activated, these proc­
esses are realized (function) 
within normal limits of physio­
logical fluctuations (see Figure 
1 graph a). When the adapto­
genic factor is present (inade­
quate conditions in the envi­
ronment) the amplitude of oscil­
lation in the alternation of the

“ Erwin Bauer (1890-I938). Austro-Hungarian biologist, defined the essence of life as a steady non-equilibrium 
state. According to the Bauer’s "principle of the permanent non-equilibrium of living matter", the particularity of 
the life events is maintained by the substances exchange processes in the living organisms which need the constant 
energy consumption: “Living systems could never be in equilibrium, they constantly use their “free” energy, 
working against equilibrium, determined by the physical and chemical lows, actual for their current environment 
(E. Bauer “ Theoretical Biology”. Moscow-Leningrad, 1935, page 43).
Erwin Bauer formulated two general biological lows:
1. Development of biological systems is the result of increasing of their external working effect (the organism's 
impact on environment) in response to the stimulus (unit of energy), received from environment. For this 
reason, biological systems able to maintain the constancy of their structure independently form external envi­
ronment.
2. Since the biological systems are constantly working and destructing, they must be able to recover themselves, 
bringing from environment all necessary materials, energy and information. Thanks to this auto-restoration 
process, biological systems maintain the “anti-entropic” condition in relation to the environment which they 
live.
506

=====PDF 518 / p.507=====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
energetic and plastic providing functions increases. However, it is only up to a certain physio­
logical limit after which there inevitably is a disturbance in the adaptational mechanism (Bauer, 
4, Kasnacheev, 59). However, in separate stages one or another process can dominate, and even 
in micro intervals of time, a balance between them is maintained.
Management of the adaptation process is done by the CNS (Figure 2).
The first results of this activity appear in the activation of specific homeostatic reactions (Figure
2). When the strength (level) of the irritants is not high and the changes in the external and inter­
nal environment is not great, and in the presence of the previously worked out adaptation to a 
given action, the adaptational effect is limited to the specifics of the homeostatic reactions. Ful­
fillment of these reactions, the same as in any life activity, requires energy and plastic provi­
sional functions.
The first to begin this task is fulfillment of the energy capabilities and plastic reserve of cell 
function. However, according to the amount of increase in strength and duration of the influence 
and the intensity of the life activity acts that are fulfilled, the energy and plastic capabilities of
Figure 2 - The scheme of the mechanism of general adaptation (Viru, 1981)
507

=====PDF 519 / p.508=====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
individual cells require support from the side of general mobilization of the energy and plastic 
reserves of the body. This means mobilization of the non-specific component of adaptation or 
(according to Viru) inclusion of the general adaptation mechanism.
Activation of the non-specific component of adaptation appears as the basic sign of the stress 
state, i.e., the state of the body characterized by the display of the general adaptation mechanism 
which ensures the positive background for realization of specific homeostatic reactions and mo­
bilization of the defensive effort by the body (Meerson. 75, 76, 77, Viru, 32, 291. Yakovlev, 
144).
In this way the basic component of the general adaptation mechanism appears as mobilization of 
the energy resources of the body and the energy provision function, mobilization of the plastic 
resources of the body and adaptive synthesis of enzymes and structural proteins. It also includes 
mobilization of the defense abilities of the body. These components are directed by the interac­
tion of different hormonal systems and the immediate nervous influences, including the nerve- 
trophic action and activation of the trophic systems (Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Haydarliu, 124, 
Kassil, 62, Kassil et al., 61. Meerson, 77).
In mobilization of the energy resources of the body and in the energy provision function, pre­
dominant importance is given to the sympatho-adrenal system, the influence of which is reached 
in the tissues with the help of its hormonal (adrenaline) and mediatory (noradrenaline) links. 
Mobilization of the plastic reserve of the body under stress is a function of the hypophyseal- 
adrenocortical system. It is locked in with the creation of a free amino acid reserve for the plas­
tic ensuring function, that is, adaptive synthesis of proteins (Viru, 32, 289, Viru. Kirge, 35, Ya­
kovlev, 144).
One of the essentials of adaptational restructuring is that in the adaptive body, there is increased 
power of the mechanism of the hormonal - humoral regulation (Viru, 32, 291, Bunt, 166, Ver- 
voom, 287, Kasssil, 61). This gives advance notice of the exhaustion of resources during long 
term hyper-functioning and with this, makes it possible to create the ability to adequately supply 
long maintenance hormonally. In addition, it increases the maximum reaction of the body to limit 
loads, that ensures maximum mobilization of its functional capabilities (Viru,32, 291, Booth, 
160, Galbo, 203, Viru, Kirge, 35, Kassil, 60, Kassil ed al. 61, Haydarliu, 124).
It has been proven that the unique correct path to the formulation of effective practical principles 
of sports training is through the clarification of the laws of human body adaptation to loaded 
muscular activity as well as the laws of the process of achieving sports mastery (PASM) in line 
with the analytical conclusions of multi-year practical experiences (Verkhoshansky, 21, 25, 
Verkhoshansky, Viru, 28, 286, Yakovlev, 139, 143).
The vastness and basic orientation of the scientific search in this area and their methodological 
hierarchy have already been determined (Verkhoshansky, 21. 24 - 27).
The general laws of PASM are first of all determined by the laws of development of the adapta­
tional process related to sports activity (Figure 3).
To a good extent, an increase in sports mastery is determined by a whole line of factors—socio­
economic conditions, effectiveness of the theoretical concept of training, professional mastery of 
the coach, the individual psycho-physiological personality traits of the athlete and so on. How-
508

=====PDF 520 / p.509=====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
Figure 3 - The principal structure of the fundamentals of the Theory and Methodology of Sport Training
ever, even with the indubitable significance of these factors, they are secondary. They can be 
looked at (and realized) under the process of PASM, but do not determine the principle mecha­
nisms of its development.
The general laws of the PASM reflect the necessary structure of multiyear training in an objec­
tive manner, including the order of development of all of its components and the principles of 
their interactions. Here we have in view the laws of the morpho-functional specialization and the 
formation of technical-tactical mastery. The methodological ideas and their organization are ab­
stracted from all the joint parts of the PASM laws, the principles of training etc. In turn, these 
principles are joined with the objective display of the practical realization of the laws of adapta­
tion of the body to loaded muscular activity, to determine the organizational-temporal form of 
constructing sports training (Verkhoshansky, 26, 27).
1. Specific essentials of the adaptation process during sports activity
Development of long term adaptation during sports activity reveals many specific traits. Clarifi­
cation of these traits has great significance in the formation of the theoretical understanding of 
PASM and the methodological principles of training
509

=====PDF 521 / p.510=====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
1.1. 
Understanding compensator}' adaptation
Short term adaptation transitions gradually into long term on the basis o f multiple short term and 
systematic training effects on the body (training days, training sessions). In this, there is multiple 
short term repetition of the excess distribution of the body's plastic reserves that are used for re­
pair of the physiologically worn out structures, as well as for adaptive synthesis of structural and 
enzymatic proteins, ensuring temporary increases in the ability of the cells to do more active 
functioning. As a result of long term repetition, the effects of these changes are strengthened and 
become more expressed. In this way, in place of the temporary redistribution of the plastic re­
serves of the body during short term adaptation, there is development of stable, stronger reforma- 
tion-long term adaptive restructuring (Verkhoshansky, Viru. 28 Viru. 32).
In the foundation of temporary over-distribution of the plastic reserves of the body are the com­
pensatory mechanisms, that is, familiar reactions directed to maintaining the necessary level of 
body functioning during inadequate conditions that are sufficient for development of a stable 
form of adaptation. The compensatory mechanisms are dynamic and quickly rising physiologi­
cal means of breakdown in order to provide for the body in extreme conditions and to gradually 
extinguish these means according to the amount of development of stable long term adaptation. 
In as much as these mechanisms precede the latter, they can be looked at as pre-adaptation ap­
pearances (Kusnetzov, 68).
In this way there is a greater base on which to speak of the compensatory adaptation that appears 
as a quality prerequisite and condition for development of stable long term adaptation (Verkho­
shansky, 25). The latter can have a progressive character if the training influence is stressful and 
brings about systematic disturbance of body homeostasis, and if the morphological restructuring 
of the body in the process of compensatory adaptation appears to be sufficiently substantial, in 
order to significantly influence the established external and internal relationships of the body, it 
brings the body to a new, higher level of special workability (Verkhoshansky, Viru. 28, 286).
1.2. 
Current adaptation reserv es of the body
The phase of compensatory adaptation is characterized by intense mobilization of the energy and 
plastic reserves of the body. This phase cannot be long. The accumulation in the body of worn 
out and “defeated" structures requires higher mobilization of the plastic reserves which leads to a 
decrease in the effect of the external work. After some time, the body recovers its functions up 
to a level which significantly surpasses the initial (Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Viru, 289). This 
signifies restoration of its adaptation potential and its readiness to once again accommodate reor­
ganization to extreme influences (Verkhoshansky,Viru, 28, 286).
This is the beginning hypothesis of the current adaptation reserve (CAR), which the body always 
has available for extreme situations that may arise requiring maximum functional loading (Verk­
hoshansky, 1985- 24, 1988 - 282, 1993 - 27). This means that the body is always ready to re­
spond to stronger external influences with adequate accommodation restructuring and to move 
on to a new functional level of motor abilities (Verkhoshansky, Viru. 28, 286). The volume of 
CAR has a definite limit, which is conditional (as determined from specialized studies) based on 
two factors: the adaptation (functional) reserve of the sympathetic-adrenal and hypophysial - 
adrenocorticoid systems (Viru, 32), and the absolute level of adaptation (morpho-functional) re­
structuring. which has already been realized in the body at the present time (Verkho-
510

=====PDF 522 / p.511=====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
shansky.Viru, 28, 286). With an increase in sport mastery, that is, according to the degree of ap­
proaching the genetically conditioned limit of adaptation capabilities, the volume of CAR de­
creases (Verkhoshansky, 24, 27, 282).
The task of compensatory adaptation is locked into the use of CAR for maintaining the hyper 
functions (Verkhoshansky, 25, 26, 27). The realization of CAR to the limits that it can be with­
stood, activates the genetic apparatus of inner cellular regulation, which carries with it activation 
of nucleic acid synthesis and proteins in the cells of the organs and systems that answer to adap­
tation. Such activation leads to the formation of structural (morphological) changes, that mainly 
increase the functional power of these systems, ensuring the transition from short term adaptation 
to long term (Meerson. 76-77, Viru, 32,33). In this, there is restoration of the adaptation reserves 
of the body, which in turn, prepares it for a new hyper-function that is, to engage extreme condi­
tions (Verkhoshansky,Viru, 28, 286).
As brought out earlier, the presence of the adaptation reserve in the body is seen in cases of acci­
dents (wrecks) (Yakovlev, 137, Prokop, 258, Beckman, 154, Letunov, 154, Garkavi, 42). Fre­
quently, even at the end of the 1950's, the concept of adaptation energy (adaptation ability) dis­
bursement during stress, together with its possible restoration, w'as used to explain the dynamics 
of sports achievements during training. Three phases were determined:
1. Phase of adaptation (increase in the athlete's abilities);
2. Phase of the highest sports workability;
3. Phase of readaptation (Prokop. 258)3.
As specialized studies (Mironenko, 82, Antonova, 1, Hachatrjan, 126, Nikitin, 88, Vrublevsky. 
39, Ganchenko, 40, Dubinin, 51. Dushenkov, 52) and sports practice (see the reviews in the 
books of Verkhoshansky: in Russian. 20, 24, 25; in Italian, 281; in English, 282, in Spanish, 284, 
in German, 293 and 294, in French. 295 ) have shown, the volume and intensity of concentrated 
training loads mastered by present day high level athletes, in exhausting CAR, the body trans­
forms itself, on average, after 18-24 weeks. In this case, further increases in loads can lead to a 
disruption in adaptation.
Strength (magnitude), volume and duration of the training influences that are needed for full 
value realization of CAR have their own corresponding quantitative significance. If the strength 
(magnitude), volume and duration of the training influences are below the necessary (optimal) 
amounts, CAR will not be realized; if they go above it, it leads to extreme exhaustion of the re­
serve capabilities. In both cases, the resulting training effect will be low (Verkhoshansky,Viru, 
28, 286).

1.4. 
Specificity of protein synthesis during adaptation
Systematic loaded muscle activity is tied in with greater mobilization of energy resources that 
require activation of the plastic provision function of the body (Meerson, 76, 77, 78, Yakovlev, 
144, 124, Panin, 94, Viru, 289). The plastic provisions include renewal of proteins, strengthening 
cell structure functioning, long term synthesis of enzymatic proteins and the protein synthesis 
necessary for the amino acids and precursors of nucleic acid (Viru, 32, Kassil, 60,61, Yakovlev, 
140, 144, Haidarliu. 124, Viru, 288. Breitbart et all, 163).
Synthesis of proteins is provided for by the genetic program coordinated in the nucleus of the 
cell. Its realization activates the action of the inductors (Yakovlev, 144. Viru, 291, Booth, 160, 
Miwa et all, 247, Horton, 227, Bylund-Fellenius, 169, Breitbart et all, 163). The basic inductors 
appear to be the cell metabolites (products of substance exchange in the cells) and hormones, 
reaching the cells via the blood (Poortemans, 257, Viru. 289, 32).
Metabolites determine the specific character of the protein synthesis; synthesized are those pro­
teins which are primarily destroyed, and likewise enzymes catalyzing biochemical reactions, ly­
ing in the base of the corresponding functions. With this, specific correspondence between func­
tional activity and adaptation of protein synthesis is ensured. Hormones as a rule strengthen 
adaptive protein synthesis, inducted by metabolites (Yakovlev, 138, 139, 140, Viru, 32, 291, 
Viru, Kirge, 35, Haidarliu, 124).
Thus, the catabolic processes that take place in the muscles during the time of work determine 
the specific character of the following biosynthesis of the substances destroyed during muscular 
activity, that is, the specificity of the anabolic processes that take place in the post work period 
(Yakovlev. 144, Breitbart et all, 163, Booth et all, 159).

In all cases, a role is played by enzyme synthesis, the preferred recruitment of which reflects the

ity (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, Kirge, 35, Viru 291).
As a result, the muscles acquire the functional properties corresponding to (adequate for) the 
work regime in specific sports activities. Thus, in the muscles, there is either strengthening of the 
anaerobic (creatine kinase and gylcolitic) resynthesis of ATP and speed of the contractile process 
progresses, or there is an increase in the respiratory resynthesis of ATP with an increase in en­
durance for long term work, or there is an increase in the mass of the contractile proteins and 
their ATP activeness, which leads to an increase in strength, or in the end result, to some degree 
of development of all of these qualities.
With this, the structure of the muscle changes in different ways. Under the influence of endur­
ance exercises, muscle mass and thickness of the muscle fibers (their perpendicular cross sec­
tion) practically does not change and because of this, there is a substantial increase in the total 
content of the sarcoplasm and myoglobin proteins, and the number of mitochondria and their 
area significantly increases.
In training w'ith speed exercises there always is an increase in muscle mass and thickness of the 
fibers. There is an increase in myofibril protein content (which also includes myosin), sar- 
coplasmatic proteins and myoglobin . The number of mitochondria and their area, increase but 
less than under the influence of exercises for endurance. But the level of sarcoplasmatic reticu­
lum proteins increases substantially (Yakovlev, 140, Viru, 289).
It is interesting that in this and other situations, new mitochondria have different functional prop­
erties, giving them the character of the training loads used. As a result of changes in the compo­
sition of the mitochondria, there are also different changes in their ability to oxidize different 
substrates. For example, the ability of mitochondria to oxidize pyruvic acid in training for endur­
ance is two times higher than in speed training (Yakovlev, 144).
In this way the specificity of the adaptive protein synthesis is expressed both in relation to the 
cell structure as well as to the type of muscle fibers. In endurance training, it is obvious that 
preference is given to the synthesis of mitochondrial proteins, and frequently to the oxidative and 
oxidative-gylcolytic fibers. It is most certain that the specificity is determined by the local ac­
cumulation of metabolites, acting as inductors of synthesis of a limited number of proteins. 
Products of mitochondria breakup can enter into a number of metabolites, acting as specific in­
ductors (Viru, 289).
Strengthened adaptive protein synthesis, realized during the time of restoration (Millword,244, 
Seene et al., 270, Wenger et al., 292), is combined with intense degradation of proteins (Viru, 
Kirge, 35, Viru,32, 291). As a result, there is strengthened renewal of the molecular composition 
of muscle proteins in order to eliminate physiological wearing out of the structural elements and 
to guarantee a high reliability of their function. Stronger degradation of the contractile proteins 
is especially expressed after long term execution of exercises for endurance.

This repression can either limit the ability to synthesize some kind of protein or lead to the fact

tions. But under the influence of certain functions - trophic influence of the nervous system or 
some kind of change in the conditions, the existing suppression can be lifted and then the muscle

In the process of sports training the muscular system becomes specialized, accommodating to the 
work executed (Yakovlev, 144, Viru,289, Miwa et al., 247). It either strengthens the capabilities 
of the anaerobic (creatine kinase and glycolytic) resynthesis of ATP and make greater progress 
in speed of movement, or there is an increase in the respiratory resynthesis of ATP and greater 
endurance for long term work, or there is an increase the mass of the contractile proteins and 
their ATP activity which leads to an increase in strength or in the end result, development of all 
of these qualities to some degree (Yakovlev, 144, Horton, 227, Booth et al., 159, Holloszy,

1.5. 
Essentials of the constructive effects of the adaptational process
The foundation for the development of the adaptational process in sports activity is the strength­
ened synthesis of structural and enzymatic proteins in the actively functioning cells. This is car­
ried out through the structural reformation toward greater functional power of the cell structure 
and with this, the tissues, organs and the entire body (Yakovlev, 140, 144. Viru. 32, 289, 291, 
Viru, Kirge, 35, Bylund-Fellenius et al., 169, Booth, 160). The pathway to stronger and purpose­
fully directed synthesis of proteins in the body takes place from the short adaptive reactions in 
long term adaptation (Meerson, 74, Viru, 33, 289). Strengthened protein synthesis as a natural 
life providing reaction of the body in response to extreme influences and the piling up of plastic 
process content (Meerson, 76,77, Haydarliu,124, Panin, 94) appears as a constructive effect of 
the adaptational process (Verkhoshansky, 24,25, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 28, Viru, 33).
The basis for the constructive effect of adaptation lies in three phenomena (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 
32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286):
specificity of protein synthesis in the after work period, conditioned by the character of the 
work executed, its intensity and means of energy provision,
- 
supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates 
serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins),
- 
a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the 
muscular work.
In this way, the known laws of development of the adaptational process during sports activity 
makes it possible to speak of two levels of the constructive effect. (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, 
Verkhoshansky, Viru, 28, 286). One of them is related to the well known phase of restitution that 
is inherent in the phenomenon of supercompensation of products and energy used up in external 
work (Yakovlev, 139, 144, Viru, 289). The other level is related to the long stages of training. It 
is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a 
result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect 
(Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283).
As stated above, the phase of restitution is characterized not only by increased metabolism but 
also a higher turnover speed of the muscle proteins which ensures the renewal of the molecular 
composition of the actin - myosin complex and other muscular proteins, in order to eliminate the 
“physiologically exhausted” structural “footprints” structural elements and guarantee a high reli­
ability of the contractile function (Viru, 289, 291).
The program of biochemical changes which are carried out as a result of the muscle exercise, de­
termine the catabolic processes taking place in the muscles during the time of work. This pro­
gram is realized during the time of rest, when the processes of anabolic-biosynthesis of products 
expended during muscle activity, takes place (Yakovlev, 138, 144, Viru, 31, 32, 33, 289).

The basic inductors of protein synthesis in the muscles are those metabolites that are formed dur­
ing the time of exercise. This appearance of metabolites strengthens the influence of the induc­
tors on different hormones which are intensively formed during the time of exercise as well as 
after it (Viru, Kirge, 35, Viru, 289, Poortemans, 257).
Specific metabolites determine the recruitment of proteins, the synthesis of which is conditioned 
by the increased activity. Also ensured with this is the relationship between functional activity 
and the adaptational protein synthesis. Not only are the proteins synthesized from which the 
functional cell structure is actively formed, but also enzymes and catalytic biochemical reactions, 
lying in the base of the corresponding cellular functions (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32).
The after work activation of the nucleic acids and protein synthesis plays an important role in the 
formation of the structural “footprints” in the specific response to the adaptation systems (Meer­
son, 76). This issue has a direct relationship to the extremely important practical problem - the 
ratio between work and rest in the sports training system and. more concretely, to directing the 
flow of the biochemical processes in the phase of restitution (Yakovlev, 144, Verkhoshansky, 24, 
25).
Tied in with this, it is appropriate to give attention to two circumstances.
We have in view the prevailing presentation in practice and in the literature, of “restoration” of 
the athlete after the training loads and the methodological methods used in this.
The problem is that the accelerated extraction from the body of the metabolites due to the use of 
different types of “restorative” procedures, (that are widely recommended and used in sports 
practice) leads to a disturbance in protein synthesis and as a result, to a decrease in training effect 
of the loads and the specifics of its direction (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25).
However, it has long been known that the “tying together" link between the previous and the fol­
lowing training sessions appears to be the after-effects (structural “footprints", traces), which are 
maintained in the tissues, organs and systems of the athlete for several tens of hours.
This is one of the most important pedagogical (methodological) positions in sports training and 
appears when there is skillful organization of the “after effects" of physical exercises (Gippenrei- 
tor, 43).
Thus, the rest period (or interval of time between the previous and following training session) is 
necessary not only for achieving a state of readiness (which to a significant extent, is evaluated 
subjectively) for the following portion of the training loads, but mainly for realization of the after 
work specific protein synthesis (Verkhoshansky, 25, 26, 27).
This leads to the conclusion that the metabolite dispersal from the body during the rest intervals, 
is in principle, not expedient because it liquidates the results of the previous load influence. This 
conclusion has especially important significance for forming the scientific bases of contemporary 
theory and methodology of sports training and shows up in the priority direction of the needed 
scientific research in this area (Verkhoshansky, 27).
The second circumstance is tied in with the so-called, principle o f complexityn , which implies 
the use of only “complex" loads or the “complex” form of training session. 30 years ago such 
forms of training were considered as progressive principles of organization of the training (Oso-

main metabolites and products of cell breakdown, produced in the process of muscular work. 
Metabolites determine the specific recruitment of proteins synthesized in the after work period. 
Ensured with this is the correlation between the increased functional activeness and specificity of 
the adaptational protein synthesis. Consequently, the training influence on the body should over­
see induction of the adaptive synthesis of protein in correspondence with the training task with 
the help of primarily single directed loads. “Complex” loads (especially, when these loads are 
used in the so-called “developmental" training sessions12) are not advisable, because it is tied in 
with great, and (which is the essence of the matter), unjustified loss of energy, that does not 
ensure the specific effect of protein synthesis (Verkhoshansky, 26, 27).
Training can be considered effective when the loads bring about induction of adaptive protein 
synthesis in the desired direction. The criteria for such loads should (or can) be the accumulation 
of metabolites or the changes in the hormonal ensemble, necessary for specific induction of the 
adaptive synthesis of protein and for its strengthening (Viru, 289).
Together with this, it is important to give attention to the need for determining the best time 
(moment) for the repeat work, in relation to the time of development of the post training protein 
synthesis. In other words, each following training session (or training load portion) must be 
started only at the moment when the protein synthesis, ensured by the preceding training session, 
is finished, or when the intensity of this protein syntheses start to decrease. If the following 
training session is carried out sooner (or too late), the main part of the positive influence of the 
preceding training session will not by realized. (Viru, 289, 290, 291).
Everything that was said above makes it possible to review the obsolete principles of training 
load organization in microcycle coming from the conception of Periodization of Training, intro­
duced by L.Matveev13, and working out contemporary models of programming the microcycle, 
based on the conception of Programming of training14 (Verkhoshansky, 27).
12 “Developmental” training sessions are the training sessions with the high level loads.
13 Matveev L.P. “The problem of periodization of sport training’*, Moscow, “ Physical Culture and Sport”, 1965. 
(MaTBeeB Jl.Fl. npo6jie.via nepHozunauHit cnopTHBHofi TpeHnpoBKH. - M.: Q hC, 1965).
The difference between the two conceptions Periodization and Programming is based on the different “vision’* 
of the training process and different approach to its planning.
According to the conception of Periodization, the training process is seen as "the chain of the microcycles", that is, 
an additive formation, "the whole” which is “the sum of its parts". The microcycle represents its base structural 
element. In fact, the most important objectives of the research, based on this conception, were finalised to elabo­
rate upon the models of microcycles for each type of training period in the sport discipline. After, the training 
process (the training plan) could be “constructed” from these microcycles, as from the "bricks" of the different 
calibre, situated in an undulant tier on the axle of the time toward the date of the competition. In regards to the day 
of competition, we were unable to predict the level of the athlete’s performance, but we must assure its constant 
(persistence, incessant) increase and we must try to obtain the maximal “angle” of this increase.
According to the conception of Programming, the training process is seen as the hierarchical system of training in­
fluences on the organism, organised over time, which can only be diversified within the microcycles. So, the train­
ing process is the "whole" which "is greater than the sum of its parts". Each change in the contents and in the se­
521

=====PDF 533 / p.522=====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
The consequent (second) phenomenon of the constructed effect of adaptation is tied in with a 
number of criteria of the post training process of restitution (the phenomena of supercompensa­
tion).
If during the time of muscular work the processes of breakdown and oxidation dominate, that is, 
processes necessary for energy provision, then during the time of rest, restoration of that which 
was used up is required. The program of synthesis taking place during the time of rest is deter­
mined by the type of break-up reaction which took place during the time of work. In this way, 
any kind of break-up reaction brings about productive resynthesis reactions in the body (rule of 
V.Engelgard). In this way, in normal functioning biosystems the restorative process is always 
potentially greater and supersedes the processes of breakdown (the phenomena of supercompen­
sation).
It has frequently been shown that a onetime 
stress influence of the catabolic phase is fol­
lowed by an anabolic phase, that is, general­
ized activation of nucleic acid and protein 
synthesis. This phase can potentiate realiza­
tion of the interrelationships between the 
functions and the genetic apparatus, and in 
this way, the structural consequences are 
formed in the systems, specifically answering 
to the adaptation to a definite factor of the 
surroundings (Meerson, 76, 77).
Thus, during a one time emotional-painful 
stress type influence (trials on animals) right 
after the catabolic effect in all the studied or­
gans, the laws of development in the activa­
tion of biosynthesis and an increase in content 
RNA1' which in turn, leads to the biosynthe­
sis of protein (Figure 5).
It has been established that the stage of post 
stress activation of the biosynthesis of RNA 
and protein, is first of all many times longer 
than the stage of biosynthesis depression and 
secondly, it is characteristic to see a substan­
tial increase from the initial level.
quence of microcycles changes "the whole", provoking the phenomenon of "emergence’’ (new properties arising in 
systems as a result of the interactions at an elemental level). So, the most important temporal measure of the train­
ing process is not the microcycle, but the Great Adaptive Cycle. A microcycle represents the working forms of the 
organization of the temporary parts of the general volume of the loads (necessary to reach the planned final result); 
the tier of which is determined by the general strategy of their distribution over time.
15 RNA (Ribonucleic acid) is a type of molecule that consists of a long chain of nucleotide units. RNA is tran­
scribed from DNA by enzymes called RNA polymerases and is generally further processed by other enzymes. 
RNA is central to the synthesis of proteins.

=====PDF 534 / p.523=====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
This stage ensures a sufficiently long period of preparation during which the organs and systems 
can respond to the physiological loads faster and more significantly activate biosynthesis and 
correspondingly, faster formation of the needed structures. These changes are much greater than 
can be produced in conditions of sharp loads in the absence of an increased fund of prepared ri­
bosomes and increased activity of the entire protein-synthesizing apparatus (Meerson, 76).
Even before this it had been shown that in the process of physical work, the biochemical shifts 
that take place in the body during the period of rest become normalized, going through a series of 
phases which include the phase of supercompensation of those ingredients that were expended. 
This pertains to the substrates serving as sources of energy as well as the different structural and 
enzymatic proteins (Yakovlev, 138).
For example, the content of glycogen 
which is decreased after physical 
work during the time of rest, in­
creases not only to the initial, but to a 
higher level (Figure 6). After this, it 
decreases to the beginning level (and 
even somewhat lower), and a new but 
already smaller increase above the 
initial levels and finally, establish­
ment of the level which existed be­
fore work (Yakovlev, 144).
Thus after work, during the time of 
rest, not only is the pre-work state of 
the muscles restored (and the body as 
a whole) but for some period, condi­
tions for increased workability are 
created. In this, the amount of super- 
compensation and the speed of its appearance, is directly related to the intensity of the expended 
products during the time of work, and the duration of maintaining this phase, from the absolute 
amounts of expenditure range from several hours to 1-2 days).
The law o f supercompensation also applies to creatine phosphate, the enzymatic and structural 
proteins, to the phosolipids, and to a number of mitochondria in the muscle fibers - in a word, for 
all products and structures, which to one or another degree, were expended or destroyed during 
the muscular activity and are resynthesized during the time of rest (Yakovlev, 144).
The phase of supercompensation appears as a first step in adaptation of the body to muscular ac­
tivity (Yakovlev, 138). Regardless of its short term (from several hours to 2-3 days), it is ensures 
execution of the following loads in conditions that are more favorable to the body.
