    20	**When to apply** — When reading or teaching the history of periodisation, and when a "loss of sports form" phase is treated as a fixed calendar step rather than as the result of a spent reserve. Inference: the footnote gives a reason to plan the "readaptation" phase by the state of the athlete, not by date.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The footnote is a one-line attribution with no evidence and no page reference into Matveev's book, and it is not signed; it reads as Verkhoshansky's side in a long dispute with Matveev (see [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]]). Matveev's own account of where the phases came from is not given. Rated `untested`. Inference: whether Matveev offered "any kind" of physiological explanation would need his 1965 book, which is not in this library.

    13	
    14	# Three Adaptation Strategies: Moderate Loads, High Loads Spread Evenly, High Loads Concentrated (Fig 4)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.3, "The adaptation strategy," Verkhoshansky defines strategy as "a form and means of realizing the laws of adaptation in practical sports conditions" and gives "three variants of adaptational strategy that have been studied and written up (figure 4)" (Verkhoshansky, 24; Verkhoshansky & Viru, 28, 286) (9.1 §1.3, PDF 522-524 / p.511-513, checked against the page images):
    17	- **A, low-middle loads.** "If moderate volume and intensity training loads are used (in relation to the current state of the athlete) then for specialized workability (W) it is characteristic to have moderate and relatively balanced development." "Full exhaustion of CAR does not take place and the adaptational process is extended over time. This type of strategy is for beginning and mid level athletes." Afterwards W can go three ways: "a decrease (if there is a decrease in the strength of the training influences), stabilization (if so called maintenance loads are used) or further increases (if the strength of the training influences are increased)" (PDF 523 / p.512).
    18	- **B, high loads distributed evenly**, "the traditional variant of organization of high level athlete training." It "ensures periodic short term disturbance of the constant internal body environment"; the process is "on a more intense level and its duration has a definite limit." Afterwards only two ways: "a decrease (even if the volume and intensity of the loads increases)" or "stabilization (if maintenance loads are used)" (PDF 523-524 / p.512-513).
    19	- **C, high loads concentrated in a short period.** "The beginning stage of training is distinguished by systematic long term and deep disturbance of body homeostasis due mainly to the mobilization of the energy resources," seen as a "steady decrease in specialized workability (W)." Then, "as a result of mainly mobilization of the plastic resources," comes "a sharply expressed increase," to "a significant increase above the initial level and even the level achieved in the first two variants." Afterwards: "a decrease (if once again concentrated load volumes are used)" or "continued stabilization (if maintenance loads are used)" (PDF 524 / p.513).
    20	
    21	Figure 4 (PDF 523 / p.512, values read from the image): panel A has no numeric scale. In B, W% rises from 100 to about 140 by week 10 and levels near 150 by week 20. In C, W% falls to about 80 near week 5, crosses 100 near week 9, and levels near 155 by about weeks 17-20. Each panel ends in tails a and b (A also c) after week 20. Each panel also carries hatched down-arrows and open up-arrows, with no legend (see "Why it works").
    22	
    23	**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's mechanism is the energy-plastic alternation (see [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]]): in A "consecutive alternation of moderate activation of the energetic (solid line) and plastic (dotted line) reserves"; in B "the expenditure of the energetic resources (solid lines) is compensated for by the mobilization of the plastic resources (dash lines)"; in C a long energy-dominated phase is followed by a plastic-dominated phase (PDF 523-524). Figure note: the text refers to solid, dotted and dash lines, but the printed Fig 4 shows one curve per panel with hatched and open arrows and no line legend. Inference: the down-arrows stand for energetic mobilisation and the up-arrows for plastic mobilisation.
    24	
    25	**When to apply** — Use A for beginners and mid-level athletes, where CAR need not be exhausted. Use C only where the athlete is highly qualified, the block can be protected from competition, and a planned dip in W is acceptable. In every variant, plan what follows the block: maintenance loads hold the level, and in B even more load does not raise it.
    26	
    27	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the C-over-B claim is the same claim the existing 6.8.1 entry carries, which Issurin (2016) contests for team, combat and swimming sports (see [[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]]). Fig 4 is a schematic: there is no sample, sport or test named for W, and A has no scale. Inference: the planned dip of about 20% in C would collide with a competition schedule in a field sport. Eric's review: Eric's stated preference differs from both B and C: "waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: that is a difference in approach to record, not a conflict over the same claim.
    28	
    29	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own contrast in Fig 4 (PDF 523 / p.512): over the same 20 weeks, B rises steadily to about 150%, while C first drops to about 80% and then finishes near 155%.

    13	
    14	# What Breaks Down During Work Decides What Is Built After It: Metabolites Induce Adaptive Protein Synthesis, Hormones Amplify It
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Yakovlev and Viru throughout (9.1 §1.4, PDF 524 / p.513, checked against the page image): "Synthesis of proteins is provided for by the genetic program coordinated in the nucleus of the cell. Its realization activates the action of the inductors." "The basic inductors appear to be the cell metabolites (products of substance exchange in the cells) and hormones, reaching the cells via the blood." "Metabolites determine the specific character of the protein synthesis; synthesized are those proteins which are primarily destroyed, and likewise enzymes catalyzing biochemical reactions, lying in the base of the corresponding functions." "Hormones as a rule strengthen adaptive protein synthesis, inducted by metabolites." His summary: "the catabolic processes that take place in the muscles during the time of work determine the specific character of the following biosynthesis of the substances destroyed during muscular activity, that is, the specificity of the anabolic processes that take place in the post work period" (PDF 524 / p.513). He repeats it later in 1.4: "Metabolites accumulated at the time of work, acts as inductors of adaptive protein synthesis. Hormones actively secreted in these conditions strengthen protein synthesis, specifically directed by metabolites, and assures the supplying of this process by 'constructive materials'" (PDF 528 / p.517).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Two supporting pieces on PDF 527 / p.516. Gene repression: the muscle fibre carries the genes for all its proteins, but "part of the genetics can be 'repressed'"; under "trophic influence of the nervous system or some kind of change in the conditions, the existing suppression can be lifted and then the muscle can synthesize the proteins, which before this, were not capable of being synthesized" (Yakovlev, 144). Glucocorticoids: they mobilise protein, create "a reserve of free amino acids for ensuring the plastic functions," and move amino acids from one tissue to another, so "the plastic reserves of the cells can be exhausted in some tissues because of the stronger slow of plastic materials" (printed so; Inference: probably "outflow") "and in others as a consequence of more intense use of free resources in the anabolic processes" (Viru). Footnote 9 (PDF 528, quoting Viru 1995, ch. 8) gives the proposed signal: "low molecular weight products of protein degradation" acting on transcription, with specific activation if they "are protein specific fragments."
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky draws the programming rule from it (PDF 532 / p.521): "Training can be considered effective when the loads bring about induction of adaptive protein synthesis in the desired direction. The criteria for such loads should (or can) be the accumulation of metabolites or the changes in the hormonal ensemble, necessary for specific induction of the adaptive synthesis of protein and for its strengthening (Viru, 289)." Inference: pick the session's means so the breakdown it causes is the breakdown of the structures you want rebuilt.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The section is a review of cited work (Viru, Yakovlev, Booth, Poortemans and others) with no data on the page. Inference: modern muscle biology also gives a large role to mechanical signalling, which this metabolite-and-hormone account does not mention, so treat it as one part of the mechanism. The page names no practical measure of "the accumulation of metabolites" or "the hormonal ensemble," so the effective-load criterion cannot be applied directly in a weight room.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own strength case (PDF 528 / p.517): hypertrophy from strength training "is based on the strengthened protein synthesis ... and is combined with an increase in the protein content, in mainly the myofibrils," and "the anabolic acting androgenic hormones strengthen this aggregate change (Viru, 33)."

    26	**Related** — [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]], [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]], [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes]] (6.12.2; 9.1 rejects "complex" loads because they do not give a specific protein-synthesis effect, PDF 532 / p.521)

    13	
    14	# Each Training Direction Builds Its Own Proteins: Speed the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum, Strength the Contractile Proteins, Endurance the Mitochondria (Table 1)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.4, PDF 525 / p.514, checked against the page image): "The specific character of the biochemical adaptation in the process of training depends to a significant degree, on the essentials of the training loads used (Yakovlev, 140)." Table 1, "Specific influence of different regimes of muscle work on the adaptive synthesis of proteins (According to A. Viru, 1995)," read from the image:
    17	
    18	| Primary direction of the training influence | The specific character of the adaptational protein synthesis |
    19	|---|---|
    20	| Development of speed | Synthesis of proteins in the sarcoplasmatic reticulum |
    21	| Development of strength | Synthesis of contractile proteins |
    22	| Development of endurance | Synthesis of mitochondrial proteins |
    23	| Development of speed endurance | Synthesis of proteins with buffering properties, synthesis of isoenzymes resistant to lower pH |
    24	
    25	The text below the table restates it by exercise type: "In strength exercises, the myofibril protein synthesis appears to be foremost. In short term exercises of maximum effort there is synthesis of sarcoplasmatic reticulum; in submaximal exercises tied in with insufficient satisfaction of the needed oxygen, accumulation of non-oxidized metabolites, and a change in pH to the acid side, there is synthesis of glycogen and protein enzymes, that have great buffering capabilities and in long duration exercises based on aerobic energy exchange, there is synthesis of mitochondrial proteins" (PDF 525 / p.514).
    26	
    27	**Why it works** — The mechanism is local metabolites acting as specific inducers (see [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]): "It is most certain that the specificity is determined by the local accumulation of metabolites, acting as inductors of synthesis of a limited number of proteins" (Viru, 289; PDF 526 / p.515). The result: "the muscles acquire the functional properties corresponding to (adequate for) the work regime," either faster anaerobic ATP resynthesis and contraction, more respiratory ATP resynthesis and endurance, or more contractile protein and strength, "or in the end result, to some degree of development of all of these qualities" (PDF 526 / p.515).     28	
    29	**When to apply** — Choose the session's dominant regime by the protein you want built. Inference: for a football lineman a heavy strength day (contractile protein) and a repeat-sprint day with short rest (buffering capacity) aim at different machinery, which supports keeping each session's main emphasis clear.
    30	
    31	**When NOT to apply** — Table 1 is a four-row summary from Viru's 1995 book, with no data, loads or durations; it names a primary product, not the only one. The speed row says speed training builds sarcoplasmic reticulum, but the next page also has speed training increasing "muscle mass and thickness of the fibers," myofibril protein, "sarcoplasmatic proteins and myoglobin" (PDF 526 / p.515), so the rows overlap in practice. The "two times" pyruvate figure is a single citation without units or method. `supported`, not `proven`, under this book's rule for findings shown without data.

    33	**Example** — The book's own pair (PDF 526 / p.515): under endurance exercise, fibre thickness "practically does not change" while mitochondrial number and area rise significantly; under speed exercise, fibre thickness always rises and sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins rise "substantially," while mitochondria rise "less than under the influence of exercises for endurance."

# Strength-Training Hypertrophy Without Matching Mitochondrial Growth Lowers Mitochondrial Density and Brings Faster Fatigue Under Endurance Loads

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.4, PDF 528 / p.517, checked against the page image): "In strength training (in contrast to endurance training) reworking of the contractile fibers takes place in the skeletal muscles without a corresponding increase in synthesis of the mitochondrial proteins and with adequate increases in the vascularisation of the muscle tissues. ######## claim--strength-hypertrophy-dilutes-mitochondria-and-speeds-endurance-fatigue.md

# Strength-Training Hypertrophy Without Matching Mitochondrial Growth Lowers Mitochondrial Density and Brings Faster Fatigue Under Endurance Loads

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.4, PDF 528 / p.517, checked against the page image): "In strength training (in contrast to endurance training) reworking of the contractile fibers takes place in the skeletal muscles without a corresponding increase in synthesis of the mitochondrial proteins and with adequate increases in the vascularisation of the muscle tissues. As a result, there is expressed hypertrophy, an increase in muscle mass of the tissues and a decrease in specific density in the mitochondria (Wenger et al, 292, MacDougall et al., 241, Tesch, Lindeberg, 273). This leads to a decreased supply of oxygen in the muscle tissues, a decrease in the functional power of the mitochondrial system and as a result, to increased production of lactate and as a consequence, fast fatigue in endurance loads (Tesch, Lindeberg, 273, MacDougall et al., 239, Meerson, Pshennikova, 78, Pshennikova, 99)."

**Why it works** — The chain on the page: contractile protein grows, mitochondrial protein does not keep pace, so the same mitochondria are spread through more muscle; less oxygen is used per unit of tissue, more lactate is made, and fatigue comes sooner in endurance work. Translation note: the page prints "with adequate increases in the vascularisation," but the "decreased supply of oxygen" that follows only makes sense if vascularisation does not keep up. Inference: probably "without adequate increases."

**When to apply** — When a strength phase precedes or overlaps a conditioning target in an athlete who needs repeated efforts: plan for the hypertrophy to cost some local oxidative capacity unless conditioning work is kept in. Eric's review: the baseline treats this kind of pairing as a programming constraint: "Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: this page gives one mechanism for why heavy hypertrophy work and endurance work compete.

**When NOT to apply** — The effect is dilution from hypertrophy; it does not apply to strength gains made with little size gain. Within this book the authors elsewhere cite research that strength training raises haemoglobin and myoglobin and helps distance sports ([[claim--strength-training-raises-haemoglobin-myoglobin-and-aids-distance-sport]], 4.4). The two are not the same claim: 4.4 is about strength training's net effect on distance performance, 9.1 is about mitochondrial density after "expressed hypertrophy." Record the difference; it is not marked `contested`. The cited studies (MacDougall, Tesch and Lindeberg, Wenger) are named but their data are not shown here.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own contrast, same page and the next: strength training gives "expressed hypertrophy" and lower mitochondrial density, whereas "training for endurance is not combined with general hypertrophy of the skeletal muscles and an increase in the myofibril mass" but with "an expressed increase in the number and size of the mitochondria" (PDF 528-529 / p.517-518).

**Related** — [[claim--strength-endurance-hypertrophy-and-cyclic-endurance]] (5.2.5, the authors' rule that excess hypertrophy hinders cyclic endurance), [[claim--endurance-training-builds-mitochondrial-protein-without-hypertrophy]], [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]], [[claim--strength-training-adds-connective-tissue-that-can-impair-fine-control]], [[framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy]]
######## claim--strength-training-adds-connective-tissue-that-can-impair-fine-control.md

# Strength Training Also Builds the Connective Tissue Around Muscle Fibres, and Too Much of It Can Make Muscles Thick and Less Fit for Fine, Varied Movement

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Yakovlev (144) for each point (9.1 §1.4, PDF 528 / p.517, checked against the page image): "In a loaded muscle, there is an especially strong break-up of proteins in the isometric regime, and at the time of rest, their synthesis is more significantly displayed. But, besides the synthesis of the contractile muscle fibers there is intense protein synthesis of the connective tissue surrounding the muscle fibers. For muscle work, these excessively developed connective tissue layers not only are not needed, but are even harmful: the muscles become thick, unsuitable for different fine, varied and precise variations in their activity." The same paragraph gives a non-contractile change in the other direction: "Strength training leads mainly to a significant increase in the content of the elastic myostromins in the muscles, structural proteins taking part in muscle relaxation," which "serves to more fully and quickly relax the muscles after their contraction." Footnote 10 (PDF 528) glosses myostromin as "a protein found in muscle stroma, the supporting framework of muscle."

**Why it works** — The page gives the observation and its consequence, not a mechanism. Inference: the link to the isometric regime suggests long, high-tension holds are the case where the connective-tissue response is largest, since that is where Yakovlev reports the strongest protein breakdown and later synthesis.

**When to apply** — Inference: in sports where fine, fast and varied muscle control matters (throwing, striking, skill positions), weigh large volumes of heavy isometric or slow high-tension work against that need, and keep speed and skill work alongside it.

**When NOT to apply** — One citation, no data, no dose: the page does not say how much training produces "excessively developed" connective tissue, nor how the "fine, varied and precise" loss was measured. The myostromin point cuts the other way (better relaxation after strength training), so the page does not support a blanket warning against strength work. Rated `untested`. Connective tissue around the fibres also transmits force and protects against strain injury (see [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]]); this claim is about excess, not about connective tissue as such.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own picture of the end state: muscles that "become thick, unsuitable for different fine, varied and precise variations in their activity" (PDF 528 / p.517).

######## claim--endurance-training-builds-mitochondrial-protein-without-hypertrophy.md

# Endurance Training Builds Mitochondrial Protein in Both Slow and Fast Fibres, Without Skeletal-Muscle Hypertrophy

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.4, PDF 528-529 / p.517-518, checked against the page images): "training for endurance is not combined with general hypertrophy of the skeletal muscles and an increase in the myofibril mass. In place of this, there is a small increase in the cell cytoplasm and an expressed increase in the number and size of the mitochondria" (Hollman & Hettinger; Saltin & Gollnick), with higher activity of "a number of mitochondrial as well as cytoplasmic enzymes." "In adaptation to work requiring endurance, hypertrophy in the muscles is not observed." As a result the muscles better "utilize pyruvate and the fatty acids," and "Endurance loads lead to an increase in the synthesis of mitochondrial proteins, to a significantly greater extent than the proteins of enzyme glycolisis and glycogenolysis (Wenger et al.,292)" (PDF 529 / p.518). "Synthesis of the mitochondrial proteins increases not only in the oxidative slow twitch muscle fibers, but also in the fast twitch fibers (Baldwin et al., 150, Yakovlev, 144)." The form of endurance that develops "is specific, corresponding to the character of the training loads (general endurance, endurance for long term work, speed and strength endurance and so on)" (Yakovlev, 137, 144; PDF 529 / p.518).

**Why it works** — Three factors, which he says "are not exclusive from one another and can be looked at as components of a single mechanism" (PDF 529-530 / p.518-519): "1. Accumulation of the recruited metabolites acting on the genetics of the cells as specific inductors of specific protein synthesis; 2. The most significant increase in degradation is of those proteins that do not appear as the decisive ones in the development of endurance; 3. The total depressed protein synthesis, on the background of which the effect of the inductors is realized and that calls forth synthesis of only proteins, is more noted in adaptation to long term muscle activity." Item 3 is garbled in translation. Inference: probably "synthesis of only certain proteins," meaning overall synthesis is held down and only the induced proteins are made. He adds that "Stronger degradation of the contractile proteins is especially expressed after long term execution of exercises for endurance" (PDF 526 / p.515), which is "one of the reasons why the strengthened adaptive protein synthesis in training for endurance does not bring about an increase in the myofibrils" (PDF 527 / p.516).

**When to apply** — When an athlete must gain aerobic capacity without gaining mass (weight-class athletes, distance athletes), or when explaining why long aerobic work does not build strength. Eric's review: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: because fast fibres also gain mitochondria by this account, aerobic work can raise the fatigue resistance of the fibres a power athlete relies on, which is consistent with that view.

**When NOT to apply** — The heart is the exception on the same page: in heart muscle there is "expressed hypertrophy." The printed sentence reads "hypertrophy in the cells of the mitochondria as a consequence of the increased size of the myofibrils" (PDF 529 / p.518). Inference: probably "the cells of the myocardium," since the sentence contrasts heart with skeletal muscle and says mitochondrial levels do not change. The claim is about adaptations from endurance training as such; it does not say mixed programmes cannot gain both. Literature summary with no data shown, so `supported`.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's tissue survey (PDF 529 / p.518): in endurance training "stronger protein synthesis is also noted in other tissues, mainly, the heart muscle tissues," and in "the brain tissues, which includes synthesis of mitochondrial proteins (Viru, 33)."

**Related** — [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]], [[claim--strength-hypertrophy-dilutes-mitochondria-and-speeds-endurance-fatigue]], [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]] (4.4, the authors' muscle-centred view of endurance), [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]
######## framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation.md

# The Constructive Effect of Adaptation Has Three Bases and Works at Two Levels: Session Supercompensation and the Long-Term Delayed Training Effect

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.5, "Essentials of the constructive effects of the adaptational process," Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519, checked against the page image): "The foundation for the development of the adaptational process in sports activity is the strengthened synthesis of structural and enzymatic proteins in the actively functioning cells." Strengthened protein synthesis "appears as a constructive effect of the adaptational process." "The basis for the constructive effect of adaptation lies in three phenomena (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286):
- specificity of protein synthesis in the after work period, conditioned by the character of the work executed, its intensity and means of energy provision,
- supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins),
- a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the muscular work."

From these he names "two levels of the constructive effect." "One of them is related to the well known phase of restitution that is inherent in the phenomenon of supercompensation of products and energy used up in external work (Yakovlev, 139, 144, Viru, 289). The other level is related to the long stages of training. It is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect (Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283)" (PDF 530 / p.519).

**Why it works** — The short level rests on restitution: the phase after work "is characterized not only by increased metabolism but also a higher turnover speed of the muscle proteins which ensures the renewal of the molecular composition of the actin - myosin complex," clearing "'physiologically exhausted' structural 'footprints'" (Viru, 289, 291). "The program of biochemical changes ... determine the catabolic processes taking place in the muscles during the time of work. This program is realized during the time of rest" (PDF 530 / p.519). Inference: the long level is the same process summed over a concentrated block; the page says only that it "is related to the long stages of training" (see [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]).

**When to apply** — Inference: use the two levels to keep two time scales apart when judging a plan. A session or microcycle is judged by restitution over hours to days; a concentrated block is judged by the delayed rise weeks after the loading, not by how the athlete performs during it.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the book contradicts itself on the second phenomenon. Here supercompensation covers "different structural and enzymatic proteins." In 1.16 the authors prefer "adaptive reconstruction," and printed p.88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" (as quoted in [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], PDF pp. 94-99). Same claim, same book. The page shows no data for either level. The link between the two levels (that the long-term effect is built from session-level restitution) is not stated on the page.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own definition of the long level: "the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads" (PDF 530 / p.519), the pattern drawn as strategy C in Fig 4 (see [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]]).

**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]] (6.10), [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the authors' names for effects on different time scales)
######## claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis.md

# Restoration Procedures That Speed Metabolite Removal Remove the Signal for Protein Synthesis, So Rest Is Mainly for Synthesis, Not Readiness

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 531 / p.520, checked against the page image) ties the work-rest ratio to protein synthesis: "The after work activation of the nucleic acids and protein synthesis plays an important role in the formation of the structural 'footprints' in the specific response to the adaptation systems (Meerson, 76). This issue has a direct relationship to the extremely important practical problem - the ratio between work and rest." He then names "the prevailing presentation in practice and in the literature, of 'restoration' of the athlete after the training loads." "The problem is that the accelerated extraction from the body of the metabolites due to the use of different types of 'restorative' procedures, (that are widely recommended and used in sports practice) leads to a disturbance in protein synthesis and as a result, to a decrease in training effect of the loads and the specifics of its direction (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25)." "Thus, the rest period (or interval of time between the previous and following training session) is necessary not only for achieving a state of readiness (which to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively) for the following portion of the training loads, but mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis (Verkhoshansky, 25, 26, 27)." His conclusion: "the metabolite dispersal from the body during the rest intervals, is in principle, not expedient because it liquidates the results of the previous load influence" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**Why it works** — The mechanism is his inducer model: metabolites formed during work are "the basic inductors of protein synthesis in the muscles" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). Clear them early and the specific signal is gone. He adds that the after-effects, "structural 'footprints', traces," are what link one session to the next and "are maintained in the tissues, organs and systems of the athlete for several tens of hours" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**When to apply** — When deciding whether to use "restorative" procedures straight after a session whose adaptation you want; the page names no specific procedure. Inference: flushing-type means such as massage, hydrotherapy or active recovery aimed at clearing metabolites are the obvious cases. Eric's review: "Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)), and "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: Verkhoshansky's position supports managing recovery through load design rather than routine post-session modalities.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested`: the book contradicts itself on the same claim. In 6.9.3 the authors report that swimmers using restoration procedures systematically during voluminous loading gained 24.2% in absolute strength and 18.9% in strength-endurance, against 7.7% and 4.9% without them (Kuchnyev 1977; Platonov 1980; PDF 368 / p.357, as quoted in [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]]). In 8.6 Talyshev's sauna and hydrotherapy straight after the workout left next-day work capacity "below its initial level," which fits 9.1, but the same therapy 6-9 hours later produced next-day "significant increase (supercompensation)" (PDF 462 / p.451, as quoted in [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]]). 9.1 calls metabolite dispersal "in principle, not expedient" with no qualifier for timing or dose. Inference: the two can be partly reconciled if procedures delayed until synthesis has run are allowed, but 9.1 does not say so. The page gives no data of its own, only his books (refs 24-27). Inference: "several tens of hours" is not a protocol; it gives no window per quality.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own statement of the priority: the rest interval is "mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis," and only secondarily for readiness, which "to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively" (PDF 531 / p.520).

**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (6.9.3 and 8.6), [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]] (8.6), [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]]
######## heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends.md

# Start the Next Session When the Previous Session's Protein Synthesis Ends or Begins to Fall, Not Sooner and Not Much Later

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Viru (289, 290, 291) (9.1 §1.5, PDF 532 / p.521, checked against the page image): "it is important to give attention to the need for determining the best time (moment) for the repeat work, in relation to the time of development of the post training protein synthesis. In other words, each following training session (or training load portion) must be started only at the moment when the protein synthesis, ensured by the preceding training session, is finished, or when the intensity of this protein syntheses start to decrease. If the following training session is carried out sooner (or too late), the main part of the positive influence of the preceding training session will not by realized" (printed so; the sense is "be realized"). He presents this, with the case against restoration procedures and complex loads, as grounds to "review the obsolete principles of training load organization in microcycle coming from the conception of Periodization of Training, introduced by L.Matveev, and working out contemporary models of programming the microcycle" (PDF 532 / p.521).

**Why it works** — The rest interval exists "mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). Load again while synthesis is still rising and the new breakdown cuts it short; wait until long after it has ended and the after-effects that link sessions, which last "several tens of hours" (PDF 531), have faded.

**When to apply** — When spacing sessions that load the same structures or quality, such as two heavy lower-body days or two speed-endurance sessions in a week. Inference: Fig 5 on PDF 533 (animal stress data, not training) shows protein synthesis peaking at about 24 and falling back toward baseline by 120-168 on its time axis (see [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]]); if that axis is hours, it would put the next hard session for the same tissues somewhere after the first day and well before a week. The page itself gives no hours.

**When NOT to apply** — No time windows, no measures and no data are given, and protein synthesis cannot be read in the field, so the rule needs a proxy that the page does not supply. It also says nothing about sessions aimed at different qualities, which load different proteins (see [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]]). Rated `untested`. Inference: in an in-season football week the game fixes most of the spacing, so the rule matters most in the off-season.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own failure case: a session "carried out sooner (or too late)" than the end or decline of the previous session's synthesis loses "the main part of the positive influence of the preceding training session" (PDF 532 / p.521).

**Related** — [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]] (8.6, timing by when work capacity is next needed), [[framework--periodization-as-additive-chain-vs-programming-as-hierarchical-whole]]
######## framework--periodization-as-additive-chain-vs-programming-as-hierarchical-whole.md

# Periodization Treats Training as a Chain of Microcycles; Programming Treats It as a Hierarchical Whole Whose Key Unit Is the Great Adaptive Cycle

**What it is** — Footnote 14 (9.1 §1.5, PDF 532-533 / p.521-522, checked against the page images; the footnote runs from the foot of PDF 532 onto the foot of PDF 533 and is unsigned) explains the two conceptions the main text names when it calls for "contemporary models of programming the microcycle, based on the conception of Programming of training (Verkhoshansky, 27)" (PDF 532). "The difference between the two conceptions Periodization and Programming is based on the different 'vision' of the training process and different approach to its planning."
- Periodization: "the training process is seen as 'the chain of the microcycles', that is, an additive formation, 'the whole' which is 'the sum of its parts'. The microcycle represents its base structural element." The plan is "'constructed' from these microcycles, as from the 'bricks' of the different calibre, situated in an undulant tier on the axle of the time toward the date of the competition." On competition day "we were unable to predict the level of the athlete's performance, but we must assure its constant (persistence, incessant) increase and we must try to obtain the maximal 'angle' of this increase" (PDF 532).
- Programming: "the training process is seen as the hierarchical system of training influences on the organism, organised over time, which can only be diversified within the microcycles. So, the training process is the 'whole' which 'is greater than the sum of its parts'. Each change in the contents and in the sequence of microcycles changes 'the whole', provoking the phenomenon of 'emergence' (new properties arising in systems as a result of the interactions at an elemental level). So, the most important temporal measure of the training process is not the microcycle, but the Great Adaptive Cycle. A microcycle represents the working forms of the organization of the temporary parts of the general volume of the loads (necessary to reach the planned final result); the tier of which is determined by the general strategy of their distribution over time" (PDF 533).

**Why it works** — The argument rests on interaction: if what a microcycle does depends on what came before and after it (as the after-effects and delayed effects in 9.1 imply), then microcycles cannot be designed one at a time and stacked. Inference: this is the same non-additivity point the authors make with their "algebraic relations" for training order in Chapter 4 (see [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]).

**When to apply** — When building an annual or off-season plan: set the overall distribution of the load volume needed for the target result first, and let the microcycles follow from it, rather than picking standard microcycle templates per period and laying them end to end. Eric's review: Eric's stated model is "waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: that is a week-level pattern repeated over a block, closer to the microcycle-as-brick view this footnote criticises, though a four-week wave can also be read as a planned whole.

**When NOT to apply** — The footnote states a view; it gives no evidence that programming plans beat periodization plans. It does not define the "Great Adaptive Cycle" here (no length, no structure on these pages). Its author is not named, and it reads as a later editorial note explaining Verkhoshansky's position; treat it as his school's view. Its picture of periodization is the critic's version; the periodisation entries in this library carry the reply (see [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]]). Rated `untested`.

**Example** — The footnote's own image of the old approach (PDF 532 / p.521): microcycles as "bricks" of different calibre laid "in an undulant tier on the axle of the time toward the date of the competition," with the aim of the steepest possible rise.

**Related** — [[principle--mesocycle-not-microcycle-as-the-unit-and-planned-dips-are-not-errors]] (6.8.1, the same rejection of the microcycle as the unit), [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]] (6.3), [[framework--pasm-laws-of-adaptation-to-temporal-forms-of-training-fig-3]], [[claim--matveev-sports-form-phases-derive-from-prokop-adaptation-energy-phases]], [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]] (4.1.2), [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]]

Accumulation of the recruited metabolites acting on the genetics of the cells as specific inductors of specific protein synthesis; 2. The most significant increase in degradation is of those proteins that do not appear as the decisive ones in the development of endurance; 3. The total depressed protein synthesis, on the background of which the effect of the inductors is realized and that calls forth synthesis of only proteins, is more noted in adaptation to long term muscle activity." Item 3 is garbled in translation. Inference: probably "synthesis of only certain proteins," meaning overall synthesis is held down and only the induced proteins are made. He adds that "Stronger degradation of the contractile proteins is especially expressed after long term execution of exercises for endurance" (PDF 526 / p.515), which is "one of the reasons why the strengthened adaptive protein synthesis in training for endurance does not bring about an increase in the myofibrils" (PDF 527 / p.516).
38	
39	**When to apply** — When an athlete must gain aerobic capacity without gaining mass (weight-class athletes, distance athletes), or when explaining why long aerobic work does not build strength. Eric's review: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: because fast fibres also gain mitochondria by this account, aerobic work can raise the fatigue resistance of the fibres a power athlete relies on, which is consistent with that view.
40	
41	**When NOT to apply** — The heart is the exception on the same page: in heart muscle there is "expressed hypertrophy." The printed sentence reads "hypertrophy in the cells of the mitochondria as a consequence of the increased size of the myofibrils" (PDF 529 / p.518). Inference: probably "the cells of the myocardium," since the sentence contrasts heart with skeletal muscle and says mitochondrial levels do not change. The claim is about adaptations from endurance training as such; it does not say mixed programmes cannot gain both. Literature summary with no data shown, so `supported`.
42	
43	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's tissue survey (PDF 529 / p.518): in endurance training "stronger protein synthesis is also noted in other tissues, mainly, the heart muscle tissues," and in "the brain tissues, which includes synthesis of mitochondrial proteins (Viru, 33)."
44	
45	**Related** — [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]], [[claim--strength-hypertrophy-dilutes-mitochondria-and-speeds-endurance-fatigue]], [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]] (4.4, the authors' muscle-centred view of endurance), [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]
46	######## framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation.md
47	
48	# The Constructive Effect of Adaptation Has Three Bases and Works at Two Levels: Session Supercompensation and the Long-Term Delayed Training Effect
49	
50	**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.5, "Essentials of the constructive effects of the adaptational process," Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519, checked against the page image): "The foundation for the development of the adaptational process in sports activity is the strengthened synthesis of structural and enzymatic proteins in the actively functioning cells." Strengthened protein synthesis "appears as a constructive effect of the adaptational process." "The basis for the constructive effect of adaptation lies in three phenomena (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286):
51	- specificity of protein synthesis in the after work period, conditioned by the character of the work executed, its intensity and means of energy provision,
52	- supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins),
53	- a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the muscular work."
54	
55	From these he names "two levels of the constructive effect." "One of them is related to the well known phase of restitution that is inherent in the phenomenon of supercompensation of products and energy used up in external work (Yakovlev, 139, 144, Viru, 289). The other level is related to the long stages of training. It is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect (Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283)" (PDF 530 / p.519).
56	
57	**Why it works** — The short level rests on restitution: the phase after work "is characterized not only by increased metabolism but also a higher turnover speed of the muscle proteins which ensures the renewal of the molecular composition of the actin - myosin complex," clearing "'physiologically exhausted' structural 'footprints'" (Viru, 289, 291). "The program of biochemical changes ... determine the catabolic processes taking place in the muscles during the time of work. This program is realized during the time of rest" (PDF 530 / p.519). Inference: the long level is the same process summed over a concentrated block; the page says only that it "is related to the long stages of training" (see [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]).
58	
59	**When to apply** — Inference: use the two levels to keep two time scales apart when judging a plan. A session or microcycle is judged by restitution over hours to days; a concentrated block is judged by the delayed rise weeks after the loading, not by how the athlete performs during it.
60	
61	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the book contradicts itself on the second phenomenon. Here supercompensation covers "different structural and enzymatic proteins." In 1.16 the authors prefer "adaptive reconstruction," and printed p.88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" (as quoted in [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], PDF pp. 94-99). Same claim, same book. The page shows no data for either level. The link between the two levels (that the long-term effect is built from session-level restitution) is not stated on the page.
62	
63	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own definition of the long level: "the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads" (PDF 530 / p.519), the pattern drawn as strategy C in Fig 4 (see [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]]).
64	
65	**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]] (6.10), [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the authors' names for effects on different time scales)
66	######## claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis.md
67	
68	# Restoration Procedures That Speed Metabolite Removal Remove the Signal for Protein Synthesis, So Rest Is Mainly for Synthesis, Not Readiness
69	
70	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 531 / p.520, checked against the page image) ties the work-rest ratio to protein synthesis: "The after work activation of the nucleic acids and protein synthesis plays an important role in the formation of the structural 'footprints' in the specific response to the adaptation systems (Meerson, 76). This issue has a direct relationship to the extremely important practical problem - the ratio between work and rest." He then names "the prevailing presentation in practice and in the literature, of 'restoration' of the athlete after the training loads." "The problem is that the accelerated extraction from the body of the metabolites due to the use of different types of 'restorative' procedures, (that are widely recommended and used in sports practice) leads to a disturbance in protein synthesis and as a result, to a decrease in training effect of the loads and the specifics of its direction (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25)." "Thus, the rest period (or interval of time between the previous and following training session) is necessary not only for achieving a state of readiness (which to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively) for the following portion of the training loads, but mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis (Verkhoshansky, 25, 26, 27)." His conclusion: "the metabolite dispersal from the body during the rest intervals, is in principle, not expedient because it liquidates the results of the previous load influence" (PDF 531 / p.520).
71	
72	**Why it works** — The mechanism is his inducer model: metabolites formed during work are "the basic inductors of protein synthesis in the muscles" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). Clear them early and the specific signal is gone. He adds that the after-effects, "structural 'footprints', traces," are what link one session to the next and "are maintained in the tissues, organs and systems of the athlete for several tens of hours" (PDF 531 / p.520).
73	
74	**When to apply** — When deciding whether to use "restorative" procedures straight after a session whose adaptation you want; the page names no specific procedure. Inference: flushing-type means such as massage, hydrotherapy or active recovery aimed at clearing metabolites are the obvious cases. Eric's review: "Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)), and "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: Verkhoshansky's position supports managing recovery through load design rather than routine post-session modalities.
75	
76	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested`: the book contradicts itself on the same claim. In 6.9.3 the authors report that swimmers using restoration procedures systematically during voluminous loading gained 24.2% in absolute strength and 18.9% in strength-endurance, against 7.7% and 4.9% without them (Kuchnyev 1977; Platonov 1980; PDF 368 / p.357, as quoted in [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]]). In 8.6 Talyshev's sauna and hydrotherapy straight after the workout left next-day work capacity "below its initial level," which fits 9.1, but the same therapy 6-9 hours later produced next-day "significant increase (supercompensation)" (PDF 462 / p.451, as quoted in [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]]). 9.1 calls metabolite dispersal "in principle, not expedient" with no qualifier for timing or dose. Inference: the two can be partly reconciled if procedures delayed until synthesis has run are allowed, but 9.1 does not say so. The page gives no data of its own, only his books (refs 24-27). Inference: "several tens of hours" is not a protocol; it gives no window per quality.
77	
78	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own statement of the priority: the rest interval is "mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis," and only secondarily for readiness, which "to a significant extent, is evaluated subjectively" (PDF 531 / p.520).
79	
80	**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (6.9.3 and 8.6), [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]] (8.6), [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]]
81	######## heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends.md
82	
83	# Start the Next Session When the Previous Session's Protein Synthesis Ends or Begins to Fall, Not Sooner and Not Much Later
84	
85	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Viru (289, 290, 291) (9.1 §1.5, PDF 532 / p.521, checked against the page image): "it is important to give attention to the need for determining the best time (moment) for the repeat work, in relation to the time of development of the post training protein synthesis. In other words, each following training session (or training load portion) must be started only at the moment when the protein synthesis, ensured by the preceding training session, is finished, or when the intensity of this protein syntheses start to decrease. If the following training session is carried out sooner (or too late), the main part of the positive influence of the preceding training session will not by realized" (printed so; the sense is "be realized"). He presents this, with the case against restoration procedures and complex loads, as grounds to "review the obsolete principles of training load organization in microcycle coming from the conception of Periodization of Training, introduced by L.Matveev, and working out contemporary models of programming the microcycle" (PDF 532 / p.521).
86	
87	**Why it works** — The rest interval exists "mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). Load again while synthesis is still rising and the new breakdown cuts it short; wait until long after it has ended and the after-effects that link sessions, which last "several tens of hours" (PDF 531), have faded.
88	
89	**When to apply** — When spacing sessions that load the same structures or quality, such as two heavy lower-body days or two speed-endurance sessions in a week. Inference: Fig 5 on PDF 533 (animal stress data, not training) shows protein synthesis peaking at about 24 and falling back toward baseline by 120-168 on its time axis (see [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]]); if that axis is hours, it would put the next hard session for the same tissues somewhere after the first day and well before a week. The page itself gives no hours.
90	
91	**When NOT to apply** — No time windows, no measures and no data are given, and protein synthesis cannot be read in the field, so the rule needs a proxy that the page does not supply. It also says nothing about sessions aimed at different qualities, which load different proteins (see [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]]). Rated `untested`. Inference: in an in-season football week the game fixes most of the spacing, so the rule matters most in the off-season.
92	
93	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own failure case: a session "carried out sooner (or too late)" than the end or decline of the previous session's synthesis loses "the main part of the positive influence of the preceding training session" (PDF 532 / p.521).
94	
95	**Related** — [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]] (8.6, timing by when work capacity is next needed), [[framework--periodization-as-additive-chain-vs-programming-as-hierarchical-whole]]
96	######## framework--periodization-as-additive-chain-vs-programming-as-hierarchical-whole.md
97	
98	# Periodization Treats Training as a Chain of Microcycles; Programming Treats It as a Hierarchical Whole Whose Key Unit Is the Great Adaptive Cycle
99	
100	**What it is** — Footnote 14 (9.1 §1.5, PDF 532-533 / p.521-522, checked against the page images; the footnote runs from the foot of PDF 532 onto the foot of PDF 533 and is unsigned) explains the two conceptions the main text names when it calls for "contemporary models of programming the microcycle, based on the conception of Programming of training (Verkhoshansky, 27)" (PDF 532). "The difference between the two conceptions Periodization and Programming is based on the different 'vision' of the training process and different approach to its planning."
101	- Periodization: "the training process is seen as 'the chain of the microcycles', that is, an additive formation, 'the whole' which is 'the sum of its parts'. The microcycle represents its base structural element." The plan is "'constructed' from these microcycles, as from the 'bricks' of the different calibre, situated in an undulant tier on the axle of the time toward the date of the competition." On competition day "we were unable to predict the level of the athlete's performance, but we must assure its constant (persistence, incessant) increase and we must try to obtain the maximal 'angle' of this increase" (PDF 532).
102	- Programming: "the training process is seen as the hierarchical system of training influences on the organism, organised over time, which can only be diversified within the microcycles. So, the training process is the 'whole' which 'is greater than the sum of its parts'. Each change in the contents and in the sequence of microcycles changes 'the whole', provoking the phenomenon of 'emergence' (new properties arising in systems as a result of the interactions at an elemental level). So, the most important temporal measure of the training process is not the microcycle, but the Great Adaptive Cycle. A microcycle represents the working forms of the organization of the temporary parts of the general volume of the loads (necessary to reach the planned final result); the tier of which is determined by the general strategy of their distribution over time" (PDF 533).
103	
104	**Why it works** — The argument rests on interaction: if what a microcycle does depends on what came before and after it (as the after-effects and delayed effects in 9.1 imply), then microcycles cannot be designed one at a time and stacked. Inference: this is the same non-additivity point the authors make with their "algebraic relations" for training order in Chapter 4 (see [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]).
105	
106	**When to apply** — When building an annual or off-season plan: set the overall distribution of the load volume needed for the target result first, and let the microcycles follow from it, rather than picking standard microcycle templates per period and laying them end to end. Eric's review: Eric's stated model is "waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: that is a week-level pattern repeated over a block, closer to the microcycle-as-brick view this footnote criticises, though a four-week wave can also be read as a planned whole.
107	
108	**When NOT to apply** — The footnote states a view; it gives no evidence that programming plans beat periodization plans. It does not define the "Great Adaptive Cycle" here (no length, no structure on these pages). Its author is not named, and it reads as a later editorial note explaining Verkhoshansky's position; treat it as his school's view. Its picture of periodization is the critic's version; the periodisation entries in this library carry the reply (see [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]]). Rated `untested`.
109	
110	**Example** — The footnote's own image of the old approach (PDF 532 / p.521): microcycles as "bricks" of different calibre laid "in an undulant tier on the axle of the time toward the date of the competition," with the aim of the steepest possible rise.
111	
112	**Related** — [[principle--mesocycle-not-microcycle-as-the-unit-and-planned-dips-are-not-errors]] (6.8.1, the same rejection of the microcycle as the unit), [[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]] (6.3), [[framework--pasm-laws-of-adaptation-to-temporal-forms-of-training-fig-3]], [[claim--matveev-sports-form-phases-derive-from-prokop-adaptation-energy-phases]], [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]] (4.1.2), [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]]
113	######## claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5.md
114	
115	# After a Single Stress, Protein Synthesis First Falls, Then Rises Well Above Baseline for Much Longer Than It Was Depressed (Meerson, Fig 5)
116	
117	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky opens the "consequent (second) phenomenon of the constructed effect of adaptation," supercompensation (9.1 §1.5, PDF 533 / p.522, checked against the page image). "If during the time of muscular work the processes of breakdown and oxidation dominate, that is, processes necessary for energy provision, then during the time of rest, restoration of that which was used up is required. The program of synthesis taking place during the time of rest is determined by the type of break-up reaction which took place during the time of work. In this way, any kind of break-up reaction brings about productive resynthesis reactions in the body (rule of V.Engelgard). In this way, in normal functioning biosystems the restorative process is always potentially greater and supersedes the processes of breakdown (the phenomena of supercompensation)." Then the evidence: "a onetime stress influence of the catabolic phase is followed by an anabolic phase, that is, generalized activation of nucleic acid and protein synthesis" (Meerson, 76, 77), and in "a one time emotional-painful stress type influence (trials on animals)" Figure 5 shows protein synthesis after the stress. "It has been established that the stage of post stress activation of the biosynthesis of RNA and protein, is first of all many times longer than the stage of biosynthesis depression and secondly, it is characteristic to see a substantial increase from the initial level" (PDF 533 / p.522).
118	
119	Figure 5 ("Dynamics of the protein synthesis in myocardium (1), brain (2) and liver (3) after the stress (Meerson, 1986)," PDF 533, values read from the image): all three curves drop at once to a trough at the "8" mark (about 64 for myocardium, 61 for brain, 57 for liver), cross 100 before the "24" mark, and peak at 24 (about 163, 158 and 181). By 48 they are near 137, 141 and 127; by 120 near 115, 118 and 107; by 168 near 107, 110 and 100. The axes carry no labels. Inference: 100 is the pre-stress level, and 8, 24, 48, 120 and 168 are hours (168 hours is one week); the time axis has breaks after 24, 48 and 120.
120	
121	**Why it works** — The page explains it by the genetic apparatus: the anabolic phase "can potentiate realization of the interrelationships between the functions and the genetic apparatus," so "the structural consequences are formed in the systems, specifically answering to the adaptation to a definite factor" (PDF 533 / p.522). The paragraph closes at the top of PDF 534 / p.523 (checked against the page image): this stage gives "a sufficiently long period of preparation during which the organs and systems can respond to the physiological loads faster," with changes "much greater than can be produced in conditions of sharp loads in the absence of an increased fund of prepared ribosomes" (Meerson, 76). The sentence introducing Fig 5 is garbled in translation ("right after the catabolic effect in all the studied organs, the laws of development in the activation of biosynthesis and an increase in content RNA which in turn, leads to the biosynthesis of protein"). Inference: it means that after the catabolic effect all the organs studied showed activated biosynthesis and higher RNA content, which then drove protein synthesis.
122	
123	**When to apply** — As the shape to expect after a single hard stimulus: a short dip, then a long overshoot. Inference: it supports spacing repeat loads for the same tissues so they land on the overshoot, not the dip (see [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]]).
124	
125	**When NOT to apply** — The data are from animals under "emotional-painful" stress, in heart, brain and liver, not skeletal muscle after training; the time course cannot be carried over to a training session without testing. Sample size and units are not given. `supported` for the pattern only. The rule that restoration "is always potentially greater" than breakdown is the supercompensation claim that the book contests elsewhere (see [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] and [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]]); Fig 5 shows overshoot of synthesis rate, not of stored content.
126	
127	**Example** — Liver in Fig 5 (PDF 533 / p.522): synthesis falls to about 57% of baseline at 8, overshoots to about 181% at 24, and is back to about 100% by 168.
128	
129	**Related** — [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16), [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]
130
